verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand, opening (mangalacharan) soratha 4, after the seven Sanskrit shlokas. Gita Press and Manas Piyush both print it as soratha 4 of the invocation, before any doha numbering begins.
attribution_note: Tulsidas's own invocation, addressed to Shiva. Some commentators read it as addressed to Shiva and Uma together (see commentaries).
translation_note: Fine. 'umā-ramana' means Uma's lord, the one who delights in Uma. That is close to 'beloved of Uma' but not the same. 'mardana mayana' is the crusher of Kama (Madana), the god of desire.
context: The Manas opens with seven Sanskrit shlokas and then five Awadhi sorathas. The first four invoke deities (Ganesha, then Vishnu in two forms by most readings, then Shiva), and the fifth bows to the guru. This is the fourth, to Shiva, who in the poem is both the first teller of Ram's story and Tulsidas's guide. Right after it the poet turns to the guru and the dust of his feet.

key_terms.sense: a body fair as the white jasmine (kunda) and the moon: soft, fragrant, cool, bright
Uma's lord, the one who delights in Uma (Parvati)
tender affection for the lowly and helpless
crusher of Kama, the god of desire

core_teaching: Tulsidas comes to Shiva as the compassionate one who loves the helpless and who mastered desire, and asks for grace before he begins. He bases his claim on his own lowliness, not his merit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, as compiled in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A prayer to Shiva alone. Each epithet points ahead to an episode the poem will tell: burning Kama, pitying the widowed Rati, marrying Uma, and then narrating Ram's story to her.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, Shivlal Pathak and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Read 'Umaraman' as invoking Uma and Shiva together, as the half-woman Lord. Janakidas adds that Parvati too 'crushed Kama', through her own renunciation.
The jasmine and moon qualities (softness, coolness, nectar, light) all serve others without any motive. So the poet trusts that Shiva will show him the same unmotivated grace.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and another note, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two similes voice the poet's wish that his own heart become soft as jasmine and clear as the moon. By naming Shiva's love for the 'dīn', he claims kinship through his own helplessness.

practical_reading: Teachers read the line as a way to ask for help from honest need rather than from merit. Admitting that you feel small is treated as the opening, not the obstacle.
misreadings: Not a rejection of love or marriage: commentators square 'Uma's lord' with 'Kama's crusher' as love without craving, or as a prayer that the poet's own heart be freed of desire.
Not a sectarian statement: the opening sorathas honour several deities in turn.
cautions: A devotional prayer. A secular reader may need the context that this is the poet asking for grace before a large task.
speaks_to: feeling small or unqualified before a big piece of work
needing to ask for help
starting something creative
people drawn to Shiva as the compassionate one
not_for: someone who wants practical steps rather than prayer
a reader put off by devotional address
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 1 (Gita Press reprint, archive.org OCR text) read directly. Growse (1883, 6th ed.) renders the same sense.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 3, chaupai 4 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush numbers the half-lines as 3.7-8). Reference matches.
translation_note: Acceptable. 'Satsang' in Tulsidas means the company of saints, the holy, and hearing Hari-katha with them. It is narrower than 'good company'. The second clause literally says it is not easily had without Ram's grace. 'सोइ फल सिधि' can be read as 'that (satsang) is the fruit and the attainment'.
context: In the opening salutations Tulsidas compares the gathering of saints to the sacred confluence at Prayag and says its effect is immediate: crows become cuckoos and herons become swans. Valmiki, Narada and Agastya told how it changed them, and whatever wisdom, fame or good end anyone has reached came through it. This line follows. The next line says even rogues are reformed by such company.

key_terms.sense: company of the holy, being with saints and their talk of God
discernment, the ability to tell real from unreal and right from wrong
Ram's grace, the condition for finding such company
the root of joy and well-being
fruit and flower: satsang is the fruit, all other practices only the flowers

core_teaching: Clear judgement grows from keeping holy company, and that company is itself a gift of grace. Practices are flowers, but satsang is the root and also the fruit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Reads a chain: Ram's grace brings satsang, satsang brings discernment, and discernment brings release. Grace is why everyone does not simply seek satsang. He cites parallels from Vinaya Patrika and Sundar Kand.
Without God's grace a person develops no taste for, or trust in, the words of the good. Other practices bring other fruits, but satsang depends on grace alone.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Baijnath: satsang is the root of two trees, discernment and joy. Janakidas: even knowing satsang's power is itself learned in satsang.
Renders satsang as 'intercourse with the good', attainable only by Ram's blessing. Good works are its flowers and perfection its fruit.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the people and conversations we choose. Judgement is shaped by whom we spend time with, and finding people who make us better is a grace worth recognising and seeking.
misreadings: Not a claim that people without mentors cannot think: the verse is about where discernment grows.
Not a call to cut off ordinary friends. Manas Piyush also notes that a brief meeting is not enough: the Manas elsewhere stresses long association (Garuda's doubt clears only after long satsang).
cautions: For someone isolated by illness, grief or circumstance, 'without satsang there is no discernment' could feel like a judgement. Frame it as an invitation to seek company, not a verdict.
speaks_to: choosing friends and community
feeling foggy or easily swayed
recovering after bad influences
gratitude for a mentor or circle that changed you
not_for: someone who has no access to company right now and would feel blamed
a reader being pressured to leave friends or family

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 3, chaupai 5 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush half-lines 3.9-10). Reference matches.
translation_note: Good. 'शठ' is the fool or rogue. 'बिधि बस' means by fate or force of circumstance, not by choice, and the commentators lean on that point.
context: This continues Tulsidas's praise of the saints: satsang is the root of joy, and the gift of grace. Here he gives its proof: it reforms the worst. He then turns to the opposite worry, whether the good are spoiled by bad company, before saying even the gods cannot fully tell the glory of saints. Doha 3 follows, bowing to the even-minded sants.

key_terms.sense: the foolish or wicked are reformed
the touch of the philosopher's stone, which turns iron to gold
by fate, through no choice of their own
the jewel in a cobra's hood, which never takes on the poison

core_teaching: Holy company can transform even the worst, as the philosopher's stone turns iron to gold. And when circumstances force good people into bad company, they keep their own nature, like the jewel in a serpent's hood.

commentaries.gist: Offered as proof that company alone, with no other practice, perfects a person.
'Reformed' means their standing rises: honour in this world and a good end hereafter.
'By fate' means the good never seek bad company. They are born into it or bound to it, like the gem born in a snake. Prahlad and Vibhishana are his examples. The gem even counteracts the poison.
Same sense: the wicked reformed like vile metal touched by the philosopher's stone. A good man fallen by mischance into evil company still keeps his virtue, like the gem in a serpent's head.

practical_reading: The verse is used both to encourage people who are trying to change through better company and to steady those stuck in difficult surroundings: you do not have to become what is around you.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay in a harmful or abusive environment: the second half describes unchosen circumstance (बिधि बस), and the commentators stress that the good do not choose bad company.
Not a claim that good people are immune to influence. It describes what the truly good do, as an ideal.
cautions: Someone living with an abusive family member could hear 'keep your nature like the jewel' as advice to endure. Pair it with the fact that the text speaks of circumstance, not of choosing to stay.
speaks_to: wanting to change and seeking better company
being in a workplace or family whose values you do not share
hope for someone who has gone astray
not_for: someone in danger who needs to leave, not endure
a reader who would hear 'the wicked' as a label for themselves without the hope of the first half

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 6 (Gita Press numbering). Reference matches. Growse's translation numbers it Doha 7, because his numbering differs early in the book.
translation_note: Fine. The text says 'sant' (saints) rather than 'the wise'. 'बारि बिकार' is the water of fault or corruption.
context: After bowing to saints and, wryly, to the wicked, Tulsidas says the Vedas and Puranas describe creation as virtue and fault kneaded together, and lists pairs of opposites. This doha sums it up. The next line adds that a person turns from fault to virtue only when the Creator grants such discernment.

key_terms.sense: the lifeless and the living, all of creation
made of virtues and faults mixed together
the saint as the swan (hamsa), which in legend can drink the milk out of milk mixed with water

core_teaching: The world is a mixture of good and bad. The mark of a saint is the discernment to take the good from everything and leave the rest.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Scripture can name the virtue and fault in each thing, as an expert can tell water in milk. Only the saint actually separates them and takes the good. Compare Bharat as swan (Ayodhya 232).
The doha works as a definition of a saint: one who stays clear of faults in this world and takes up only virtues.
The Creator made the universe of animate and inanimate, good and evil. A saint, like a swan, extracts the milk of goodness and rejects the worthless water.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for how we look at people and situations: notice what is good in a person or a place and take that, rather than feeding on faults.
misreadings: Not a call to deny real harm or wrongdoing: the text admits faults exist.
Not license to judge others as 'water'. The discernment is for what one takes in, not for condemning.
speaks_to: feeling surrounded by negativity
a mixed experience: a job, family or city with good and bad in it
learning not to dwell on others' faults
not_for: someone processing a serious wrong done to them, who may hear it as 'just focus on the positive'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 8, chaupai 1 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush half-lines 8.1-2). Reference matches.
attribution_note: Listener 'all beings' is apt: Tulsidas salutes all creatures.
translation_note: Good, but it drops 'आकर चारि', the four classes of birth (from womb, egg, moisture or sweat, and seed or sprout). '8.4 million kinds' is correct for 84 lakh.
context: Before starting, Tulsidas salutes the whole of creation in several rounds: first all gods, demons, humans and creatures as pervaded by Ram, then individual groups, and here every being as full of Sita and Ram. Next he asks them all to treat him as their servant and bless him, since he has no confidence in his own wit.

key_terms.sense: four 'mines' or classes of birth: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, sprout-born
the traditional 8.4 million species of beings
full of, pervaded by, Sita and Ram

core_teaching: Seeing every creature as pervaded by Sita and Ram, the poet bows to all of them. Reverence for the divine becomes reverence for every being.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas salutes the world three ways, satisfying three schools: as Brahman (Vedanta), as individual souls, and as Prakriti with Purusha (Sankhya), hence the mention of birth-classes here.
'Ram-maya' earlier honoured the Lord's majesty. 'Siya-Ram-maya' shows the intimate form living in the poet's heart. Seeing the world so is a ripe stage of love.
Naming Sita with Ram means bowing to female and male alike, equally. It cites the Adhyatma Ramayana and Padma Purana: all that is feminine is Janaki, all that is masculine is Ram.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The verse states a Vedantic vision without asking readers to drop ritual or dismiss the gods.

practical_reading: Teachers cite it as a basis for treating every person and creature with reverence: if the divine is in everyone, courtesy is owed to everyone.
misreadings: Not a denial that harm or evil exists: in the same section Tulsidas speaks frankly about the wicked.
cautions: Mentions the 8.4 million births, which implies the rebirth cycle. That is harmless here, but readers outside the tradition may need it explained.
speaks_to: practising respect and humility
feeling disconnected from others
environmental or animal reverence
starting a day or a task with gratitude
not_for: someone who has been harmed and is being told to revere the person who harmed them

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 8, chaupai 6 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush half-lines 8.11-12). Reference matches.
translation_note: Good.
context: Tulsidas has just confessed that his wit is small and his ambition large. He asks good people to forgive his boldness as parents enjoy a child's lisp, and says the crooked will laugh, those who wear others' faults as ornaments. These lines explain the laughter. The next line compares most people to ponds and rivers that swell only with their own water.

key_terms.sense: rich with flavour, or utterly flat
excellent people, called 'sajjan' in the next line

core_teaching: Everyone finds their own work good, whatever its quality. Those who are genuinely glad at someone else's work are rare, and they are the truly good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Answers the mockers: their own verse may be flat, yet they prize it. They will never rejoice at another's verse, however fine. Manas Piyush prefers this reading.
Applies the first half to Tulsidas himself: whatever others say, everyone likes their own poem. Manas Piyush finds this fits the next half less well.
Compares it to one's own curd: nobody calls it sour. It cites Dohavali 355: no one dislikes their own conduct, just as a garlic-eater does not notice the smell.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a check on envy and self-regard: taking real pleasure in a colleague's or friend's good work is a mark of character, and it is rare.
misreadings: Not a call to stop valuing one's own work: Tulsidas goes on to write anyway, trusting the good to receive it kindly.
speaks_to: professional jealousy
creative people and critics
teams and workplaces where credit matters
parents and teachers learning to celebrate others
not_for: someone whose work was just harshly dismissed and needs encouragement, not a lesson in humility

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 8, chaupai 7 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush half-lines 8.13-14). Reference matches.
translation_note: Good. The reading 'सकृत' (one, rare) is preferred by Manas Piyush and most editors. Some editions read 'सुकृत' (meritorious). Our 'rare' follows सकृत.
context: This continues the point of the previous line, that people love their own work and seldom rejoice at another's. Tulsidas gives the image: rivers and ponds rise only with their own water, while the ocean swells when it sees the full moon. The doha that follows admits his luck is small but his hope large, trusting that the good will enjoy the poem and the wicked mock it.

key_terms.sense: rare, one in many, like the ocean
on seeing the full moon, another's fullness

core_teaching: Most people swell only at their own gain. The rare good person rises in joy at someone else's success, as the ocean's tide rises with the full moon.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Rivers and ponds overflow with a little water, while the ocean holds much without spilling. So petty people become intoxicated with a little learning, and the good, full of it, stay within bounds.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A swollen river breaks its banks and does damage, just as small people with a little wealth disregard everyone. Their flood lasts a season. The ocean's joy returns every full moon.

Pairs the images with the previous line: ponds and rivers for those who love only their own poetry, the ocean for those glad at others'. Cites Kishkindha Kand's flooded stream as a petty man made rich.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to invite readers to feel glad at a sibling's, friend's or rival's success: real joy at another's rise is the sign of a large heart.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of being glad at one's own success, only of being glad at nothing else.
speaks_to: envy at a friend's or sibling's success
comparison on social media
learning to celebrate others
mentors watching students surpass them
not_for: someone who has just suffered a real loss while others prospered, who may need comfort before a lesson

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 15, chaupai 2 (Gita Press numbering; Manas Piyush half-lines 15.3-4). Reference matches.
attribution_note: Tulsidas speaking. Shiva and Parvati are the ones he bows to, not listeners in a dialogue.
translation_note: Good. 'दिन दानी' can mean 'giving every day' or, read as 'दीन दानी', 'giver to the lowly'. Pt. Ramkumar notes the short vowel is for the metre.
context: In the opening salutations Tulsidas bows in turn to Brahma and then to Shiva and Parvati, before Vishnu's forms and Ram's family. This pair of lines comes in that series. Right after it he praises Shiva and Parvati for the Shabar mantras made for the good of the world in the Kali age.

key_terms.sense: kinsman or friend of the lowly
who gives daily, or gives to the lowly

key_terms.term: सेवक स्वामि सखा सिय पी के
key_terms.sense: servant, master and friend of Sita's beloved, Ram
well-wishers without guile or ulterior motive

core_teaching: Tulsidas names Shiva and Parvati as his own teacher and parents, the friends of the helpless who give every day. They wish him well without any motive, and they stand to Ram as servant, master and friend.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guru because Shiva teaches what is good for us. Mother and father because they do us good. Kin to the helpless, and providers who sustain. The poet says they wish him well in every way, the world in one way.
Ties the line to the tradition (Mool Gosain Charit) that Tulsidas's parents abandoned him at birth (Vinaya 275) and Bhavani fed the infant. Hence 'father and mother' carries personal weight.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on 'servant, master, friend'
commentaries.gist: The Manas shows Shiva as Ram's servant (bowing to him), as master (Ram worships him at Rameshwaram) and as friend. The name Rameshwar is read all three ways.

practical_reading: Readers use it to name where they found care when human parents or teachers were absent, and to see a divine source of steady, unmotivated goodwill.
misreadings: Not a slight on human parents: it describes Tulsidas's own life and devotion.
cautions: The traditional backstory of Tulsidas being abandoned by his parents comes from a later hagiography (Mool Gosain Charit), which scholars treat as tradition rather than verified biography.
speaks_to: people without parents, or estranged from them
gratitude toward a teacher who was like a parent
devotees of Shiva and Parvati
feeling looked after despite being 'lowly'
not_for: a reader in fresh grief for a parent who may not want a substitute offered

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 21, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 21, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.19: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Mostly right. The last clause says that when the name is remembered, the form itself comes into the heart with special love. Our translation keeps the love but drops 'the form comes'. Our_note has it right.
context: Tulsidas is in the long praise of Ram's name (Bal Kand 19-28). Here he argues that name and form are two adjuncts of the inexpressible Lord, and that the form depends on the name. He goes on to say the name is a witness and interpreter between the formless and the embodied God.

key_terms.sense: lying in the palm of the hand
remember, call to mind, the name

core_teaching: Even something in your hand cannot be recognised without its name. But remembering the name, even without seeing the form, brings that form into the heart with love. That is why Tulsidas puts the name above the form.

commentaries.gist: Proof within the Manas: Hanuman did not recognise Ram until Ram told him his name (Kishkindha Kand), and then he fell at his feet.
Call a name among sleepers and only that person answers. The form, with all its qualities, lives subtly within the name, and praising the name pleases the one named.
Shows Tulsidas's philosophical skill. Without names nothing can be known or told apart: someone who knows the shapes but not the names will mix up a mango and an amla.
Same sense: without the name the form is not recognised even in your hand, but meditating on the name without seeing the form fills the soul with devotion.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to explain why calling a loved one's name, or God's, brings their presence near even when they are absent or unseen.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of the form or of images. Tulsidas says both are the Lord's, and he will go on to praise the form.
speaks_to: missing someone far away or gone
a devotee who cannot visit a temple or see the deity
people starting name-repetition (japa)
not_for: a reader who wants a practical rather than devotional reflection

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 21 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 21'). NOT 1.19: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good.
context: This doha closes the stretch on name and form in the praise of Ram's name (Bal Kand 19-28). Next Tulsidas turns to the four kinds of devotees (yogis, seekers, the distressed and the wise) who all reach their goal through the name.

key_terms.sense: Ram's name as a jewel-lamp, a lamp that needs no oil and cannot be blown out
the tongue as the threshold of the door, the mouth

core_teaching: Keep Ram's name on the tongue like a jewel-lamp on a threshold. Like a lamp in a doorway, it lights both the inner life and the outer world.

commentaries.gist: Why a jewel-lamp? An oil lamp can run dry or blow out, like other practices that need money and are upset by desire and anger. The name, like a gem's light, cannot be extinguished. It should never leave the tongue.

commentaries.who: Vedanti Bhushan Pt. Ramkumar Das, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Dehari' means threshold, by the Amarakosha: body as house, mouth as door, tongue as the sill where the lamp sits. Manas Piyush agrees and cites the 'threshold-lamp' maxim of light on both sides.
Reads 'dehari' as a lamp-stand. The tongue holds the name as a stand holds a lamp, and should be used for nothing else. Manas Piyush rejects this sense as unattested in lexicons.
Translates it as placing Ram's name like a jewelled lamp at the door of the tongue, for light within and without.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage japa through the day, at work, on the road, at home, so that one practice brightens both inner peace and outer conduct.
misreadings: Not a magic formula that removes outer problems by itself.
speaks_to: inner darkness or confusion
wanting a simple daily practice
keeping steady speech and thought at work
not_for: someone in acute crisis who needs practical help first

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 27, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 27, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.25: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good. 'जग जाला' is the net of the world, the pairs of opposites and entanglements.
context: Tulsidas compares the ages: in the first age the Lord was pleased by meditation, in the second by sacrifice, in the third by worship. The fourth, Kali, is rooted in impurity, with minds swimming like fish in a sea of sin. In such a terrible time, he says, the name is the wish-fulfilling tree. The next line adds that in Kali the name is the only support.

key_terms.sense: the net or tangle of worldly life
giver of what one rightly wishes
well-wisher for the next world, father and mother in this one

core_teaching: In a hard age the name of Ram grants what one truly needs and frees one from the world's tangle. It cares for a person here and hereafter as parents care for a child.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Here the name's greatness is shown through time: in every age and every world, those who repeat it became free of sorrow.

commentaries.who: Shri Sudarshan Singh, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The name grants wishes the way parents do: it guards your ultimate good and refuses what would harm you, as parents deny a sick child bad food. Compare Narada's story (Bal Kand 133).
A wishing tree gives wealth, duty and pleasure but not liberation, and grants even harmful wishes. The name differs on both counts. 'Remembering' means no effort: the net of opposites dissolves.
In these fearful times the name is the only tree of life, and meditating on it stills all commotion.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reassure people who feel the times are against them: the simplest practice, remembering God, is enough to begin, and it looks after what is truly good for you, not just what you want.
misreadings: Not a promise that every wish will be granted: the commentators stress it gives like a parent, withholding what harms.
Not a reason to skip medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: The surrounding verses describe the Kali age bleakly. Keep the focus on the comfort, not on 'the age is sinful'.
speaks_to: feeling overwhelmed by the times
wanting a simple practice
needing to feel parented or protected
not_for: someone awaiting a specific outcome (a diagnosis, a job, a court ruling) who may hear a promise

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 27, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 27, half-lines 7-8'). NOT 1.25: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good. Kalanemi is Ravana's uncle, who disguised himself as a sage to delay Hanuman (Lanka Kand) and was seen through and killed.
context: This continues the praise of the name in the Kali age, after the line calling the name a wish-tree and a parent. Tulsidas says the paths of earlier ages (rites, devotion, knowledge) are out of reach, and the name alone supports. The doha that follows compares the name to Narasimha protecting Prahlad.

key_terms.sense: ritual action, devotion, discernment: the classic paths
the one support, something to lean on
the demon who disguised himself as a holy man to trick Hanuman
the clever and capable Hanuman, who saw through the disguise

core_teaching: When the usual spiritual paths feel out of reach, the name of Ram is still a support. And when the age deceives, the name sees through it, as Hanuman saw through Kalanemi.

commentaries.gist: Rites need wealth and correct procedure, devotion needs a pure mind, and knowledge needs dispassion and restraint. All are hard when minds are restless. The name has none of these preconditions.
'No karma': people have fallen from their duties. Good deeds are done for praise, worship is outward show, and knowledge is mere words. So the name is the only real recourse.
Kali is deceitful. It knows the name's power, so it attacks by trickery, as Kalanemi did in a sage's disguise. The name, like Hanuman, sees through and destroys the deceit.
The three paths denied here (discernment, action, devotion) are the meditation, sacrifice and worship of the earlier ages named just before.

practical_reading: Teachers offer it to people who feel they 'can't do' spirituality (no time, no discipline, no learning): one simple remembrance is still open to them.
misreadings: Not a rejection of ethical action, devotion or study: it is a claim about the easiest refuge.
cautions: Depicts the present age as degraded. Avoid framing the reader's own life as corrupt.
speaks_to: feeling unable to keep up any practice
burnout, exhaustion, depression that make discipline impossible
feeling deceived or manipulated
not_for: a reader who would hear 'no devotion, no discernment' as a judgement on themselves

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 28, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites it as '28. 1'). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good.
context: This is the last line of the long praise of Ram's name. Having said the name works in every age, Tulsidas says it works whatever the mood in which it is said. He then bows to Raghunath and begins, confessing his faults and trusting Ram to set them right.

key_terms.sense: with good feeling or ill feeling
good in all ten directions, everywhere

core_teaching: Whatever the mood in which the name is said, with love, with ill will, in irritation or in laziness, it brings good everywhere. Its power does not depend on the speaker's state.

commentaries.gist: Four modes: 'bhav' is loving relationship (servant to master, child to parent), 'kubhav' hostile feeling like envy or enmity, 'anakh' anger from a love that has turned sulky, 'alas' the name slipping out in grief or fatigue.

commentaries.who: Vijay Dohavali, as cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Gives examples: Shiva repeated the name with love, Valmiki with 'wrong' feeling (the reversed name), Kumbhakarna in sloth, and Ravana in anger.
'Kubhav' also covers self-seeking motives, repeating it for show, joking, or mere semblance of the name. Even these are not wasted.
Renders it as repeating the name 'whether in joy or in sadness, in action or in repose', bliss spreads all around.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to tell people not to wait until they feel devout: begin the practice tired, irritable or doubtful, and keep going.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of careless or mocking use of sacred names: it praises the name's generosity.
Not a claim that inner feeling does not matter at all: the Manas elsewhere prizes loving remembrance most.
speaks_to: feeling too low, angry or tired to pray
guilt about a half-hearted practice
restarting a practice after a lapse
not_for: someone who needs to hear that their feelings matter, not just the ritual
readers who feel pressured into religious practice

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 28, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 28, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good. 'निज दिसि देखि' means looking from his own side, at his own nature, not at the servant's merit.
context: Having bowed to Raghunath and begun, Tulsidas lists his own shortcomings. His mind and wit are poor, his poetry lacks every grace, his fortune is small. He trusts that Ram, whose kindness never tires, will set everything right. The next lines describe how a good master accepts his servant's honest effort, and Ram most of all.

key_terms.sense: he will set right what is spoilt in me
whose kindness is never sated with being kind
a good master and a bad servant
looking from his own side, at his own nature
the treasury of compassion has nurtured me

core_teaching: Grace does not wait for the servant to deserve it. Ram cares for Tulsidas by looking at his own compassionate nature, not at the servant's poor record, and his kindness never tires.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'He will set right' assumes something is spoilt, and earlier lines say what: mind and wit, the poetry's craft, and luck. 'In every way' means all of these will be mended.
Once grace is given it keeps growing. If a devotee errs, the Lord thinks he gave too little grace and takes the fault on himself.
Reads 'अघाती' also as 'अघ-हाती', the destroyer of sin: without his grace no other god's favour removes wrongdoing.
Other masters pay by service rendered. Ram shows kindness without service. It cites Kavitavali: at Ram's door alone the poor, the weak and the wayward are called in and honoured.

practical_reading: Teachers use it with people weighed down by their own failings: grace is not a wage for good behaviour, so one can start from where one is.
misreadings: Not a licence to stop trying: Tulsidas goes on to work hard at the poem.
Grace does not erase consequences or responsibility toward people one has hurt.
speaks_to: shame and low self-worth
feeling unqualified for a task
a lapse in practice or conduct
being cared for despite one's failings
not_for: a reader who would use it to excuse harm to others without making amends

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 28 (क), the first of two dohas numbered 28 (Gita Press). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good. 'सठ सेवक' is a dull or foolish servant (the poet himself). 'सचिव सुमति' are wise counsellors.
context: Tulsidas has said that Ram, a good master, accepts honest effort and looks at the heart. Now he cites the proof: the stones of the bridge to Lanka floated, and monkeys and bears became his trusted counsellors. In the next doha (28 ख) he jokes that everyone laughs at Ram for having such a servant as Tulsidas.

key_terms.sense: love and eager wish (here, to tell Ram's story)
made stones into vessels on water, the floating bridge stones
monkeys and bears made into wise counsellors

core_teaching: The one who made stones float and made monkeys and bears into wise counsellors will honour the love and hope of even a dull servant. Grace makes the unfit fit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The examples are deliberate. Telling Ram's story needs a sound mind, and his is poor. Ram gave monkeys wisdom, so he will give it too. The floating stones carried an army across, and the endless story will carry him.

commentaries.who: Sant Gursahay Lal, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Love' is his remembering the name and bowing to Raghunath before beginning. 'Liking' is his wish to be set right.
Stones that sink and drag others down were made into boats that carry others. Animals fit only to be made to dance became counsellors. If Ram did that, he will fulfil a human servant's wish.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing the Bhagavata (5.19.7)
commentaries.gist: Birth, beauty, eloquence and intellect do not win Ram's favour. He made friends of forest creatures to show it.

practical_reading: Teachers offer it to anyone who feels unqualified, whether a first-time parent, a new student or a beginner: earnest love counts, and help comes for what one cannot do alone.
misreadings: Not a slur on animals or on 'foolish' people: the point is that grace raises up whoever it touches.
speaks_to: impostor feelings
starting a creative or service project without credentials
feeling 'too ordinary' to matter
not_for: a reader who would take 'foolish servant' or 'monkeys and bears' as an insult to themselves
non-devotional readers looking for practical self-worth advice

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 29, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 29, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.27: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Acceptable. Some manuscripts read 'भोरि' (simple, innocent) for 'मोरि', which gives 'praised my simple-hearted devotion'. 'कहत नसाइ होइ हियँ नीकी' is best read as 'though it is spoilt in the telling, if it is good in the heart...'.
context: Tulsidas has just confessed that his audacity is so great that even hell would turn up its nose, and that he is afraid of his own fear, yet Ram never took notice of it even in a dream. Here he says the Lord, having heard and looked and considered, praised his devotion. The next lines say the Lord keeps no mistake in mind, and give the examples of Sugriva and Vibhishana.

key_terms.sense: hearing, looking, and weighing it with a clear inner eye
my devotion and my intent (variant: my simple devotion)
spoilt in the telling, badly expressed

key_terms.term: रीझत राम जानि जन जी की
key_terms.sense: Ram is pleased, knowing his servant's heart

core_teaching: Even when what we say or do comes out badly, Ram looks at the intention in the heart and is pleased by it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Hearing, seeing and weighing describe how the Lord takes in a devotee's devotion. 'Su-chit chakh' means considering with the mind.

Objects to the plain reading: Ram knows all and needs no hearing or seeing, and self-praise spoils merit. Reads instead: I have heard from guru and scripture that the Lord looks for the heart's clear eye.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Replies: Tulsidas is reassuring himself, not boasting to others. And love explains it all: Ram ate Sudama's rice, Shabari's tasted berries and Vidura's greens.
Though the story is spoilt by the telling, Ram accounts it good, since the will is good.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to clumsy prayers, awkward apologies and imperfect work: sincerity is what is received.
misreadings: Not an excuse for careless words toward people: it describes God's reading of intent, not a rule that others must ignore how we speak.
speaks_to: fear of saying the wrong thing
a clumsy apology or prayer
perfectionism in creative or devotional work
people with speech or language difficulties
not_for: someone hurt by another's 'well-meant' words, who may hear their pain dismissed

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 29, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 29, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.27: our id and label are off by two.
translation_note: Good. The next half-line, not in our text, completes the thought: Vibhishana did the same, and Ram never held it in his heart even in a dream. Our translation stops before saying Ram overlooked Sugriva's lapse. Our_note supplies it.
context: This continues from the line that Ram is pleased by the good in a servant's heart even when the telling is spoilt. Tulsidas says the Lord does not keep a mistake in mind and remembers the heart a hundred times. His example is pointed: the misdeed for which Ram killed Bali, Sugriva and Vibhishana later committed too, yet Ram honoured them.

key_terms.sense: a slip or mistake that has been made
remembers the heart's good feeling a hundred times
like a hunter, striking from hiding

core_teaching: The Lord does not hold on to a devotee's lapse but keeps recalling the good in their heart. The proof is that he overlooked in his friends the very wrong he punished in an enemy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A slip is an act. If word and deed go wrong but the heart is good, Ram is pleased. He cites Dohavali: what is made by the mind, Ram treats as well made.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Valmiki 2.1.11 and Gita 9.30
commentaries.gist: Ram is satisfied by a single kindness and does not recall a hundred wrongs. Whoever worships single-mindedly, even with bad conduct, is to be counted good.

Bali's sin was taking his younger brother's wife. Sugriva then took Tara, and Vibhishana Mandodari. Ram overlooked these because of their devotion. Bali, an enemy of a devotee, was punished, then forgiven when he took refuge.
The Lord is not mindful of a chance fault but always considers the heart. Sugriva and Vibhishana did what Bali was killed for, yet Ram honoured them.

practical_reading: Teachers use the first half for people stuck in guilt: God remembers your good heart more than your slip. The Bali example is usually only mentioned, not dwelt on.
misreadings: Not a model for overlooking repeated harm in human relationships, especially sexual or domestic wrongs.
Not 'mistakes have no consequences': Bali's story shows they do; the point is about the heart of one who turns to God.
cautions: The illustration involves Bali's killing and the taking of a brother's wife or widow. Handle carefully, or use only the first half for a distressed reader.
speaks_to: guilt over a past mistake
fear that one's failings define one
believers anxious about divine judgement
not_for: someone dealing with infidelity or abuse, who might hear 'forget the wrong'
a reader being pressured to forgive a repeat offender

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 58, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 58, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.54.
attribution_note: The narrator is Yajnavalkya speaking to Bharadvaja (the frame in which the Sati story is told), so 'Narrator -> Bharadvaja' is right. The second half is Sati's inner thought.
translation_note: Good.
context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. On the way home a heavenly voice praised Shiva's vow. Sati asked what it meant, he would not say, and she guessed that he knew everything. This line opens her remorse. The next line shows her realising he has withdrawn from her.

key_terms.sense: did not speak my offence openly

core_teaching: Facing what she had done, Sati is consumed with worry. She also sees Shiva's depth: he knew her fault and still did not throw it in her face.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Only now does she truly grasp her deed. Not knowing what punishment is coming makes the worry grow. A Padma Purana verse: the pyre burns the dead, worry burns the living.

Not naming her fault, lest it hurt her, is his fathomless depth. Far from punishing, he would not even say it aloud. She weighs his virtues against her failings: he all-knowing and kind, she foolish to deceive him.
It is human nature, when trouble comes, to replay one's misdeeds and panic more. She wonders what came over her to hide anything from the one who wished her well.

practical_reading: Readers take it as a picture of remorse after hurting someone who loves us, and of the grace of a partner who does not shame us even when they know.
misreadings: Not a model of never discussing problems in a relationship: Shiva's silence here is mercy, not a rule.
Not an endorsement of the 'deserved' suffering that follows: it describes what happened.
cautions: The arc ends with Sati's death at her father's sacrifice. In the preceding doha (57 क) she blames her deceit on women being 'by nature foolish', a line an editor should not carry into a modern reading.
speaks_to: remorse after lying to a partner
realising the other person knew all along
being treated more gently than one deserved
not_for: someone already drowning in guilt, unless paired with the hope of repair later in the story (Parvati)
a reader whose partner punishes them with silence, who may hear silence praised

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 58, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 58, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.54.
attribution_note: The narrator is Yajnavalkya to Bharadvaja, as in the previous line. 'Narrator -> the reader' is inconsistent with rcm.1.54.chaupai.1, which says Bharadvaja.
translation_note: Good. 'अवाँ' is a potter's kiln, which burns slowly and inside, without visible flame.
context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. Sati has just realised that Shiva knows and has spared her the shame of hearing it said. Now she reads in his manner that he has withdrawn from her. Unable to speak, she burns inside, and they sit apart on Kailash for a long time until news of her father's sacrifice arrives.

key_terms.sense: understanding the fault as her own
burns like a potter's kiln, slow and hidden

core_teaching: When we know a breach is our own doing, words fail and the heart burns quietly. The verse names that silent, smouldering remorse.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Shiva had resolved that loving Sati as before, after she took Sita's form, would break the path of devotion. Reading his face, she sees this. Her worry came from the fault, her anguish from the abandonment.

commentaries.who: Pt. Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: She is called 'Bhavani' here because, like Shiva, she is deep: though abandoned, she kept it hidden in her heart.

Reads the withdrawal as the traditional penalty: a wife who has offended is set aside rather than harmed, and for a wife no grief is greater. (A period view; editors should not carry it into a reading.)

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the silent, consuming guilt that follows a breach of trust, and why it needs to be spoken and repaired rather than left to smoulder.
misreadings: Guilt is a signal to make amends, not a sentence to burn forever.
Not a model of how to respond when a partner errs: Shiva's withdrawal comes from his particular vow.
cautions: Speaks of being abandoned by one's husband. Commentary frames it in patriarchal terms. For a reader whose partner has withdrawn, this can reinforce self-blame.
speaks_to: silent guilt after a lie
feeling a loved one pull away and knowing why
being unable to speak about one's own wrong
not_for: a reader in an emotionally abusive marriage
someone whose guilt is out of proportion and needs reassurance
research_note: Our id and label use 1.54; the Gita Press number is 1.58.2. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2, which numbers this passage the same way, and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 57 (ख), the second of the two closing verses of doha-group 57 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it as 57). NOT 1.54. It comes just BEFORE 58.1-2 in the text, not after.
attribution_note: Strictly it is inside Yajnavalkya's narration to Bharadvaja, but it works as the poet's aside on love and deceit, and is usually quoted as Tulsidas's own maxim. Acceptable.
translation_note: Good.
context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. Sati has just guessed that Shiva knows everything, and reproached herself for deceiving him (57 क). The narrator then comments with this image. The next lines show her worry and Shiva's withdrawal.

key_terms.sense: water sells at the price of milk when mixed with it
they separate and the sweetness is lost
the sourness of deceit, as acid curdles milk

core_teaching: True love lifts the lesser partner to the value of the greater, as water mixed with milk sells as milk. But a drop of deceit splits them, and the sweetness goes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Mixed with milk, water takes milk's price, colour and taste. That is milk's generosity. Once something sour falls in, the milk splits and the taste is gone: so deceit ends companionship and love.
Split milk cannot become milk again, and a torn heart does not rejoin. It cites a popular saying that pearls, milk and the heart cannot be mended once broken.
Shiva, camphor-white, is the milk, and Sati the water. United, they were worshipped and honoured as one. Deceit separated them and spoiled the union.

commentaries.who: Bhikharidas's verse, cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Milk and water show mutual love: water sells at milk's price, and when milk is heated the water burns first, and milk boils over to reach it. Each sacrifices for the other.

practical_reading: Teachers use it on honesty in close relationships: love raises us, but even small concealments sour trust.
misreadings: Not proof that trust can never be rebuilt: in the Manas itself Sati is reborn as Parvati and, after long austerity, reunited with Shiva.
cautions: Some commentary says a split heart never rejoins. That can feel like a verdict to someone who lied and is trying to repair. Pair it with the Parvati story.
speaks_to: keeping a secret from a partner
the cost of small lies
gratitude for a partner who lifts us
not_for: someone who has confessed and is working to repair trust, who may hear it as hopeless
a person being falsely accused of deceit

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 62, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 62, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.58.
translation_note: Good.
context: Daksha, Sati's father, holds a great sacrifice and invites all his daughters and their husbands except Shiva and Sati, because Daksha took offence at Shiva in Brahma's assembly long ago. Sati, longing to see her family and the festival, asks to go. Shiva says it is not right to go uninvited where you are resented. She goes anyway, is slighted, finds no share set aside for Shiva, and gives up her body in the sacrificial fire.

key_terms.sense: the home of a friend, master, father or teacher

core_teaching: One may go uninvited to a friend's, master's, father's or teacher's home. But where someone bears hostility toward you, going brings no good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: What Shiva warned came true. No one showed Sati affection, courtesy or regard: Daksha did not ask after her, and her sisters smiled mockingly.
Calling her 'Bhavani' shows he has renounced only the Sati body, not his deep love. His vow does not mean her humiliation would not grieve him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Bhagavata 4.3 and Skanda Purana
commentaries.gist: Shiva warns that she will be dishonoured because she is his. The Skanda Purana says those who enter another's house uninvited meet a humiliation worse than death.
'Shil, sneh, kani' are lost on both sides: they will not honour her, and she, slighted, will lose her composure and affection toward them.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to family gatherings and workplaces: closeness gives you a right to show up, but where you know there is active hostility, protect your dignity rather than walk in hoping for warmth.
misreadings: Not a rule to cut off family; it is a caution about walking into known hostility.
Not victim-blaming: Daksha's insult, not Sati's longing, is the wrong in the story.
cautions: The story ends with Sati's death by self-immolation at the sacrifice. Do not link the verse to that ending for a distressed reader.
speaks_to: deciding whether to attend a family event where you are resented
estrangement from a parent or in-laws
workplaces with a hostile boss
not_for: someone grieving a family rupture who wants reconciliation, not justification for distance
a reader at risk of self-harm (because of how the story ends)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 70, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 70, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.66.
attribution_note: Narada to Himavan (with Maina present), correct.
translation_note: Good. 'आसुतोष' (Ashutosh) means quickly pleased. 'किएँ कलेसू' means when hardship, here austerity, is undertaken.
context: Reading the newborn Parvati's palm, Narada said her husband would be without qualities or honour, without parents, careless, a matted-haired yogi in inauspicious dress. Her parents were devastated. Narada explains that in Shiva these marks are not faults, for the able are not tainted by them. Here he says a marriage with Shiva would be wholly good, and that if Parvati does austerity, Shiva, who can even erase destiny, will be won.
core_teaching: Shiva is hard to win, yet quickly pleased by sincere effort and hardship. What looks like bad news in Parvati's future becomes good when she seeks him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Because Shiva is the able Lord, the 'faults' Narada listed are virtues in him. 'Shambhu' means maker of welfare, so 'good in every way' fits. The earlier marriage brought separation; this one brings reunion.
Hard to win: Ravana offered his own heads. But he is also Ashutosh, so the hardship need not last long. Vinaya Patrika gives examples of how quickly he pleases.
As Tripurari he destroyed the impossible Tripura. Likewise he can wipe out what fate has written. Destiny binds those who turn from God and loosens before the devoted.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage perseverance: what seems out of reach often yields to sincere, sustained effort sooner than we expect.
misreadings: Not a promise that suffering earns rewards on demand.
'Hardship' here is chosen spiritual discipline, not enduring abuse.
cautions: The austerity that follows is extreme (Parvati gives up even dry leaves). Avoid suggesting self-deprivation.
speaks_to: a goal that feels out of reach
parents worried about a child's future
devotees of Shiva
not_for: someone exhausting themselves trying to earn love or approval

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 71 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 71'). NOT 1.67.
translation_note: Good. Our 'misuse' note cites 'Parvati's tapas, 1.68'. In Gita Press numbering that advice is at 1.72.
context: After Narada leaves, Maina weeps and begs Himavan to find a suitable husband for Parvati, even against the prophecy. Himavan replies that Narada's word cannot fail, the moon would sooner rain fire. Then he says this doha. Next he gently tells Parvati to do austerity for Shiva.

key_terms.sense: remember the Lord (with Shri, his consort)

core_teaching: Worry cannot change what is beyond our control. Remember the Lord: the one who made our child will see to her good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He says 'remember the Lord' because the Lord made Parvati. The one who creates also provides.

Himavan holds to the principle that 'he who protects the child in the womb protects it still'. Too much cleverness unsettles faith. Holding to the Lord alone, Himavan sets his own mind and his wife's at rest.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and S. P. Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Shri-Bhagavan' means the Lord with Lakshmi: pray that Parvati gets a husband as fine as Shri's. Mishra: worship with Shri fulfils every wish.
'All worry' means worry over the family and the match, over whether a fit husband will come, and over the inner burning.

practical_reading: Teachers offer it to anxious parents: do your part, but hand the worry you cannot act on to the One who made your child.
misreadings: Trust sits beside action, not instead of it: Himavan immediately advises a concrete step (Parvati's austerity, Gita Press 1.72).
speaks_to: parents anxious about a child's marriage, health or future
spousal anxiety in a family decision
worry about things outside one's control
not_for: a parent facing a child's medical emergency who needs action, not reassurance
someone being told to 'just pray' instead of getting help

attribution_note: Manas Piyush calls it 'brahma-gira', Brahma's voice. Sudhakar Dwivedi and V. Tripathi argue that 'Brahma' here means the supreme Brahman (Ram). 'Voice from the sky (Brahma)' is acceptable.
translation_note: Good. Note 'गिरिराजकुमारि' (Gita Press) and 'गिरिजाकुमारि' (dataset variant).
context: Parvati does years of austerity: living on roots and fruit, then leaves, then water and air, then giving up even dry leaves (hence the name Aparna). Her body is reduced to bones. Seeing her so wasted, a voice from the sky speaks. Then the seven sages arrive to test her resolve.

key_terms.sense: your heart's wish has borne fruit

core_teaching: Sustained devotion bears fruit. When the goal is secured, the hardship should be laid down.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The voice came because her body was so wasted it seemed life would leave it. Unlike to Manu or Ravana, it does not say 'ask a boon', because everyone knew her wish.
Second reason: she would be too shy to ask openly for a husband, as she later tells the sages with hesitation. So the voice simply announced fulfilment.
When she stopped eating even dry leaves the gods cried 'Aparna!', fearing for her life, and Brahma, amazed, spoke.

practical_reading: Readers take it as permission to stop striving once something is truly won, and as reassurance that long, faithful effort is seen.
misreadings: Not a model of starving or punishing the body to get what you want. The voice's first command is to stop the hardship.
cautions: The surrounding text describes extreme fasting until the body is skin and bone. Do not use it for readers with eating disorders or self-punishing habits, or frame deprivation as admirable.
speaks_to: the end of a long, hard effort (exams, treatment, a long wait)
permission to rest
faithful waiting finally rewarded
not_for: someone with an eating disorder or self-harm through deprivation
a reader still waiting with no end in sight, who may feel taunted
