verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 76, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 76, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.72.
translation_note: Our reading (Shiva grieves for his devotee Sati) is the main one in Manas Piyush. A minority reading (Ramcharitmanas Prakash) takes the grieving 'Bhagavan' as Ram, pained by his devotee Parvati's suffering. S. P. Mishra finds that fits the context, but Manas Piyush prefers Shiva and Sati.
context: After Sati gave up her body, Shiva wandered, repeating Ram's name, sometimes teaching sages, sometimes telling Ram's virtues. Meanwhile Parvati was born and performed her austerity. These lines show Shiva in his grief. Soon Ram appears to him and asks him to marry Parvati.

key_terms.sense: the pain of separation from a devotee

core_teaching: Even the Lord, who is free of desire, feels the grief of separation from one who loved him. He carries it by teaching and telling Ram's story.

commentaries.who: Manas Patrika, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He fills his days with Ram's story so the grief of losing his single-minded devotee does not overwhelm him. His conduct teaches: speak of Ram to a listener, listen to a speaker, and otherwise remember alone.

commentaries.who: S. P. Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Though desireless, he grieves because he knew Sati as a devotee. Mishra also reports another reading in which the grieving Lord is Ram, pained by Parvati's tapas.
Links the line to Shuka's advice: one who wants freedom from fear should hear, sing and remember Hari, depending on whether a speaker or listener is present.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say grief is not a failure of wisdom: even the wisest feel loss. Shiva's way is to keep teaching, serving and remembering.
misreadings: Not 'the enlightened do not grieve': the verse says the opposite.
Not a recipe to bury grief in busyness: it shows grief held alongside meaningful work.
cautions: Mentions the aftermath of a spouse's death (Sati's self-immolation is the backdrop). Gentle, but name the loss carefully.
speaks_to: grieving a spouse or partner
feeling that a spiritual person 'shouldn't' grieve
carrying grief while still working or caring for others
not_for: a reader whose partner died by suicide, since Sati's self-immolation is the backdrop
someone who needs permission to stop working and rest in grief
research_note: Our id and label use 1.72; the Gita Press number is 1.76.1. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2, which numbers this passage the same way, and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 78, second half of chaupai 3 plus chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 78, half-lines 6-8'). NOT 1.74. Our text starts mid-chaupai: the half-line before it is 'कहत बचन मनु अति सकुचाई। हँसिहहु सुनि हमारि जड़ताई॥'.
attribution_note: Parvati to the seven sages, correct.
translation_note: Good. Parvati's tone is self-deprecating and shy. Manas Piyush says she speaks 'with great hesitation', expecting them to laugh.
context: The seven sages (Saptarishi), sent by Shiva to test her, find Parvati as if she were austerity in person. They ask whom she worships and what she wants. Shyly, expecting to be laughed at, she says her mind is set on the impossible. The sages then mock Narada and Shiva, and she answers them point by point.

key_terms.sense: my mind has set itself stubbornly
a wall built on water, the impossible
only Shiva, always, as my husband

core_teaching: Parvati admits that by worldly judgement her hope is impossible, yet her heart holds to Shiva alone and to her guru's word.

commentaries.gist: Her hesitation: the sages asked for her secret, she is shy to speak of a husband before elders like fathers, and she expects laughter. 'Daughter of the mountain' explains the 'stone-like' stubbornness she owns to.
Reads the three images as mind, act and word: the stubborn mind, flying without wings (the deed), and 'I want Shiva always' (the speech).
Love makes one 'dull': she means she is too full of love to be reasoned with.
Some editions add a half-line 'सुनत रिषिन्ह के बचन भवानी...' before this. Manas Piyush and Gita Press treat it as an interpolation.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for quiet, self-aware commitment: you can admit something looks impossible and still choose it with your whole heart.
misreadings: Not praise of stubbornness against all advice: her steadiness rests on trust in her guru and on a worthy goal.
Not a model for pursuing someone who has said no.
speaks_to: holding to a long-shot goal
a choice of partner or vocation that others doubt
feeling foolish for hoping
not_for: someone fixated on a person who does not reciprocate
a reader whose 'resolve' is harming their health
research_note: Our id and label use 1.74; the Gita Press number is 1.78.3-4. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2, which numbers this passage the same way, and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 80, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 80, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.76.
attribution_note: Parvati to the seven sages, correct.
translation_note: Good. 'हठ' is resolve or obstinacy; here it is her own word, turned back on the sages.
context: The sages have mocked Narada's advice and listed Shiva's 'faults', then offered Parvati Vishnu, a 'better' match: handsome, pure and faultless. She laughs and answers each jibe in turn. They had said 'your body is born of a mountain', and this is her reply. Next she says she will not abandon Narada's word, for one who lacks faith in the guru's word finds no happiness.

key_terms.sense: a body born of the mountain

key_terms.term: हठ न छूट छूटै बरु देहा
key_terms.sense: the resolve will not break, though the body may
even when burned it does not give up its nature

core_teaching: Parvati turns the sages' taunt into a statement of steadiness: like gold born from stone, which only grows purer in fire, her love does not change under testing.

commentaries.gist: She concedes the sages' point and turns it: a mountain-born heart is firm like stone. Her resolve will carry into other births. She cites 'for crores of births I will wed Shambhu or stay unmarried'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on the gold image
commentaries.gist: Fire changes everything but gold, which gets brighter as it is heated. So testing only deepens her love. Compare Ayodhya 205 on gold and love.

commentaries.who: Khara and Lamagoda ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Khara: when burned, the stone gives up its hardness, but the gold born of it does not, so her father's resolve may waver but hers will not. Lamagoda: she answers in the sages' own playful tone.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to integrity under pressure: tests and criticism can refine a sound commitment rather than break it.
misreadings: Steadiness is not stubbornness; keep checking that the goal is still worth it.
Not a call to sacrifice health or life ('though the body may break') for a goal.
cautions: 'Let the body go but not the resolve' can be dangerous for a reader with self-harm or eating-disorder risk. Keep the gold image and leave out the body clause.
speaks_to: staying true to a value under ridicule
commitment to a partner or vocation others dismiss
feeling tested and refined
not_for: someone at risk of harming themselves for a goal
a person in a harmful relationship told to 'hold on'
research_note: Our id and label use 1.76; the Gita Press number is 1.80.3. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2, which numbers this passage the same way, and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 80 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 80'). NOT 1.76.
attribution_note: Parvati to the seven sages, correct.
translation_note: Good. 'Grant that' captures the concessive tone: she accepts the sages' claims for argument's sake.
context: The sages, testing her, called Shiva a house of faults and Vishnu the home of all virtues, and offered to arrange a match with Vishnu. Parvati, having answered their other jibes, closes with this. She then says that had they come before Narada she would have taken their advice, but she has given her life to Shiva. The sages, satisfied, bless her and report to Shiva.

key_terms.term: जेहि कर मनु रम जाहि सन
key_terms.sense: the one in whom a heart delights
that heart has concern with that one alone

core_teaching: Love is not a comparison of qualities. Once the heart has given itself to someone, lists of faults and virtues no longer decide anything.

commentaries.gist: She will not argue that Shiva's 'faults' are virtues, nor say a word against Vishnu. Conceding everything, she says her mind is simply absorbed in Shiva. Single-minded devotion to one's chosen deity is the lesson.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Kathasaritsagara and Parvati Mangal
commentaries.gist: 'To each, that is sweet where their mind is fixed.' Tulsidas's Parvati Mangal has her say: does one who loves count faults and virtues?
The line has become a proverb for the single-pointedness of love. Parvati's love rests on an inner bond, not outer qualities.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to devotion to one's chosen deity or path, and to committed love: loyalty does not depend on winning comparisons.
misreadings: Choosing for yourself still means listening honestly to those who care.
Not a reason to ignore real red flags such as abuse or deceit in a partner. Shiva's 'faults' here are only appearances.
speaks_to: family disapproval of a partner
choosing one's own path or faith
people pressured to 'trade up'
not_for: someone whose loved ones are warning of genuine harm in a relationship
research_note: Our id and label use 1.76; the Gita Press number is 1.80. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2, which numbers this passage the same way, and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 108, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 108, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.102.
translation_note: Good. The argument is: you are my wish-tree; I live in your shelter, so I should not stay poor in understanding.
context: After their marriage, Shiva sits under the great banyan on Kailash. Parvati, remembering her previous birth as Sati and the doubt that cost her so much, sits at his left and asks: if you are truly pleased with me and know me as your own, take away my ignorance and tell me the story of Ram. This is the start of the Shiva-Parvati dialogue that frames the Manas.

key_terms.sense: one whose home is under the wish-fulfilling tree

core_teaching: Parvati reasons that someone sheltering under a wish-tree need not suffer want, so she, living in Shiva's grace, asks him to clear her confusion. Asking honestly for understanding is itself an act of trust.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: She recalls that in her last birth Shiva neither was pleased with her nor treated her as his own, so her ignorance remained. Now that he has, she argues, ignorance has no reason to stay.
She calls him the wish-tree and 'heap of joy' because he has just honoured her. The ending confirms it: 'by your grace my sorrow is gone' (120.3). The ignorance is not knowing Ram's true nature.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Baijnath: 'your own servant' means serving in mind, deed and word. Panjabi: seating her on his left shows he has forgotten all her past offences.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Traces the stages: servant and master become student and teacher ('you are guru of the three worlds'), and the purpose is named: confusion removed, sorrow ended, joy gained.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage people to bring their doubts openly to someone they trust, especially after an old mistake. Being accepted again is the time to ask.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotees never face hardship: the 'poverty' here is confusion of mind.
speaks_to: lingering doubt or confusion about faith
returning to a teacher or partner after a past rupture
wanting to understand, not just believe
not_for: someone in material poverty, who may hear the wish-tree image as mocking
research_note: Our id and label use 1.102; the Gita Press number is 1.108.2. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 116, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites '116. 1' and numbers the half-lines 1-2). NOT 1.109 and NOT chaupai 5.
translation_note: Good. 'अगुन' is read differently by the schools (see commentaries). 'Without qualities' is the safe rendering.
context: Parvati has asked how the formless Brahman could be the prince she saw grieving in the forest. Shiva first rebukes those who confuse the two without discernment (115). He then states the principle in this line, and goes on: just as there is no difference between water and ice, the formless Lord takes form out of love.

key_terms.sense: God with attributes and form, and without
under the sway of the devotee's love

core_teaching: God with form and God without form are not two. The formless, unborn One takes on form, compelled by the love of devotees.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'No difference' means that just as the formless has no delusion or defect, neither does the embodied form, though it may seem to show grief or confusion.
Brahman always has divine qualities such as mercy and love. 'Nirguna' means those qualities are unmanifest, 'saguna' that they are manifest. One reality, two states.
Brahman is truly without any qualities, pure being, consciousness and bliss. The embodied form is how it appears. Manas Piyush sets out both readings without forcing one.
Parvati's question is shaped by her old doubt: if Shiva says the formless becomes embodied, she will see that as Sati she failed to grasp that Ram himself is that Brahman.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reconcile people who feel torn between an abstract spirituality and a personal, devotional God: the same reality is approached both ways, and love is what makes it near.
misreadings: Not a ranking of form-worship below formless meditation, or the reverse.
speaks_to: tension between philosophical and devotional faith
interfaith or inter-sect conversations within Hinduism
feeling that God is distant
not_for: a reader in acute distress who needs comfort rather than theology
people put off by doctrinal debate
research_note: Our id and label use 1.109.5; the Gita Press number is 1.116.1. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 119, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 119, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.112.
attribution_note: Shiva to Parvati, correct. 'जासु' (whose) refers to Ram.
translation_note: Good. 'बिबसहुँ' means even helplessly, unwillingly or without reverence, by contrast with 'सादर', with reverence, in the next half.
context: Shiva is answering Parvati's doubt about Ram's nature. He says that Ram, the Lord whose name he himself repeats in Kashi to free the dying, is the supreme Self. Then he contrasts the name said helplessly with the Lord remembered lovingly. He closes by telling Parvati that doubting such a Lord destroys knowledge and dispassion.

key_terms.sense: wrongs piled up over many lives
like a cow's hoofprint, a trivial puddle

core_teaching: Even saying Ram's name helplessly burns away old wrongs. Remembering him with love makes the ocean of worldly life as easy to cross as a hoofprint.

commentaries.gist: 'Helplessly' covers saying it when falling, yawning, in pain or fear, or because one is among saints, like Ajamila calling his son Narayana. Its contrast with 'reverently' gives two grades of fruit.
The name is fire and past sins are a mountain of cotton: one spark burns it all. It cites a Padma Purana verse. Saying the name and hearing it have the same fruit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and V. Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ramkumar: devotion yields the fruit of both action (sins destroyed) and knowledge (liberation). Tripathi: helpless utterance burns sin, but loving remembrance carries one across.

practical_reading: Teachers encourage people that no practice is wasted, and that loving, regular remembrance makes life's difficulties feel smaller.
misreadings: Praise of remembrance, not a promise that life's problems will vanish; practical help still matters.
Not 'past actions have no consequences in this life'.
cautions: Speaks of sins across many births, a rebirth doctrine that some readers may find heavy.
speaks_to: guilt about the past
feeling overwhelmed by life
people who can only manage a little practice
not_for: someone in acute crisis who would hear 'just remember God' as dismissive
research_note: Our id and label use 1.112; the Gita Press number is 1.119.2. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset. Manas Piyush's gloss cites a Kavitavali anecdote about a man of another faith who cried 'haram' and was saved. Editors should not reuse that example.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 120, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites '1. 120. 1'). NOT 1.113.
translation_note: Good. 'सरदातप' is the fierce sun of the autumn (Ashvin) month. Since the moon's rays relieve it, the image is precise.
context: Shiva has finished explaining Ram's nature (Bal Kand 116-119). Parvati, joyful, tells him his words have cleared her delusion. Then she asks the next questions: why the formless took a human body, and the story of the avatar, which Shiva goes on to tell.

key_terms.sense: the harsh heat of autumn sun

core_teaching: Words of real understanding cool a mind burned by confusion as moonlight relieves the autumn heat. Doubt resolved brings peace as well as knowledge.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Shiva called his words sun-rays that end the night of error. Parvati calls them moon-rays that end the day's burning. The same speech dispels darkness and soothes heat.

commentaries.who: Prof. Lala Bhagwandin, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva sees his words as removing darkness. Parvati finds they also bring peace, so she chooses the moon, which does both. She then says her sorrow has gone too.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A dissenting note: her claim is partly polite deference. Shiva later says the 'shadow' of her old delusion still lingers, so full clarity comes only with the whole story.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe the relief of a good explanation from a trusted teacher, friend or counsellor: understanding is also emotional rest.
misreadings: Not a claim that one conversation ends all doubt: the commentary notes she still needs the rest of the story.
speaks_to: relief after a long doubt is answered
gratitude to a teacher
anxiety eased by understanding
not_for: someone still in the middle of doubt, for whom the resolved ending may feel out of reach
a reader whose questions were dismissed by a teacher
research_note: Our id and label use 1.113; the Gita Press number is 1.120.1. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 133, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 133, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.127.
translation_note: Good. Our setting says Vishnu 'won't grant' the face. In the story he gives Narada a monkey's face instead: 'Hari' also means monkey. Narada is laughed at the bride-choice and curses Vishnu, which becomes a cause of the Ram avatar.
context: Narada, proud of having resisted Kama, falls in love with a princess at a bride-choice (svayamvara) staged by Vishnu's illusion. He asks Vishnu for Vishnu's own handsome form. Vishnu answers with this image of the doctor and vanishes. Narada, still deluded, does not grasp the hint and is mocked at the ceremony for his monkey face.

key_terms.sense: the physician does not give it

core_teaching: As a good doctor refuses a sick person the food that would harm him, the Lord withholds what we crave when it would hurt us. Refusal can be care.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The patient cannot tell harmful food, the doctor can. Narada is sick with desire and asks for a woman, his 'harmful food'. Vishnu says 'listen' so Narada can never say he was not told.
Calling him 'sage, yogi' is quiet irony. The yogi who boasted of conquering desire has become a 'deluded sage'.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Narada has a fever of lust with greed, and soon anger. A patient denied bad food curses the doctor, as Narada will. The good doctor bears it calmly for the patient's sake.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Shiva Purana
commentaries.gist: The same image appears there: as a fine physician helps the afflicted, because you are dear to me.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe disappointment, a job or relationship that did not work out, as a possible protection, and as a model for parents and mentors who must sometimes refuse.
misreadings: Not every refusal is for your good; this is a way to reframe, not a reason to accept harm.
Not a justification for controlling others 'for their own good'.
cautions: In the story the 'treatment' is public humiliation. Avoid implying that humiliation is good for people.
speaks_to: a rejection or closed door
craving something one suspects is bad for one
parents saying no to a child
not_for: someone being denied basic rights or care by another person who claims it is 'for their good'
fresh grief after a loss that was not a choice
research_note: Our id and label use 1.127; the Gita Press number is 1.133.1. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 142 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'soratha 142'). NOT 1.135.
attribution_note: Narration (Shiva telling Parvati of Manu). 'Narrator -> the reader' is acceptable.
translation_note: Good. 'चौथपन' is the fourth stage of life, old age.
context: Shiva tells Parvati about another cause of Ram's avatar: Svayambhuva Manu and Shatarupa. Manu ruled for ages by divine command, and his children included Dhruva's father and Devahuti, mother of Kapila. In old age he grieved that his life had passed without devotion to Hari. He handed over the kingdom and went with Shatarupa to the Naimisha forest for austerity, where Ram promised to be born as their son.

key_terms.sense: detachment from the pull of the senses
while living at home, in household life
the fourth stage of life, old age
a life gone by without devotion to Hari

core_teaching: Even a righteous life of duty can leave the heart unfulfilled. Seeing that late is painful, but it becomes a turning point toward what matters.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Two griefs: ages spent in enjoyment, and old age reached at home with life passing without devotion. He felt aversion to both and resolved to leave them. Dharma leads to detachment, detachment to devotion.
Manu cannot be called a sensualist. 'No detachment' means household life left no room for it. His remorse is shown to teach the world.

Manu kept dharma all his life, so why regret? Tulsidas's teaching: dharma brings happiness, not devotion, and without devotion there is no liberation. It cites Kavitavali: wealth and power mean nothing without love for Ram.

practical_reading: Teachers use Manu as a model for midlife and retirement reflection: a dutiful life can still lack what matters most, and it is not too late to turn.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of family or working life: Manu's rule was by divine command and righteous.
Not 'your life was wasted': his grief leads straight to fulfilment.
cautions: Can sting for an older reader who feels their life has been wasted. Pair it with Manu's turn and its fruit.
speaks_to: midlife or retirement reflection
feeling something essential was missed
transition after a long career
not_for: an elderly reader who is ill or dying and cannot 'begin again'
someone already sunk in regret without hope
research_note: Our id and label use 1.135 sortha; the Gita Press number is 1.142. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 2 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 161 (ख), the second closing verse of doha-group 161 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it under 161). NOT 1.153.
attribution_note: Tulsidas's own aside (his name is in the verse), correct.
translation_note: Good. Some commentators read 'मूढ़ न चतुर नर' as 'fools are fooled, not the clever'. Pt. Ramkumar explains the phrase as a regional idiom meaning 'not only fools, the clever too'. Our translation follows the main reading.
context: Shiva tells the story of King Pratapbhanu (who will be reborn as Ravana). Lost while hunting, the king meets an old enemy disguised as a hermit. The false ascetic wins his trust by seeming to shun fame, saying public honour is a fire that burns the forest of austerity. Tulsidas interjects with this warning. The king's trust leads to a Brahmin's curse and his ruin.

key_terms.sense: not only fools but clever people

core_teaching: A fine appearance and sweet words can deceive the clever as easily as the foolish. Judge by conduct, not by looks or speech, as the beautiful, sweet-voiced peacock eats snakes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The king was first fooled by the holy dress, now by the sweet words, hence 'nectar speech'. 'Mudh na chatur' is a Gahora idiom: fools and clever alike are fooled.
Dress and speech are fair but conduct foul, as with the wicked who speak sweetly like peacocks and devour great snakes. It cites a Dohavali couplet naming Shurpanakha, Maricha, Putana and Ravana.
A swindler first secures trust, then spreads his net, as Manthara did with Kaikeyi.
Some read 'fools are deceived, not the clever', meaning true devotees. The king, lacking devotion and craving immortality, was a fool in that sense.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to scams, charismatic fraudsters and 'godmen': polish and piety are not proof of honesty, and intelligence is no protection.
misreadings: Not a reason to distrust all religious people or all kind speech.
The peacock is an image only; no moral judgement of the bird.
speaks_to: having been scammed or manipulated
evaluating a charismatic leader or guru
shame at being fooled ('even the clever are')
not_for: someone already paranoid or isolated, who may hear 'trust no one'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 192, chhand stanza 4 (the 'bhae pragat kripala' birth hymn; Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 192, half-lines 7-8'). NOT 1.180.
attribution_note: Kausalya speaks the first half. The last line is the poet's phalashruti (the merit of singing this). Correct.
translation_note: Good. Our setting says 'cosmic form'. Strictly, Kausalya saw the four-armed Vishnu form, with the universes in every pore of his body (stanza 3).
context: At Ram's birth the Lord appears to Kausalya in his four-armed divine form. She praises him, then knowledge dawns and he smiles and reminds her of her past births' austerity (as Manu and Shatarupa). Her mind turns from awe to a mother's longing, and she asks him to become a baby. He cries like a newborn, and the queens come running.

key_terms.sense: her mind shifted, from awe to a mother's love

core_teaching: Love asks God to be near rather than grand. Kausalya prefers her child's cry to the divine form, and the Lord gladly becomes small for love.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: His smile and the story he told were meant to take away her knowledge of his godhood. Once she felt like a mother, she called him 'child' instead of 'Lord' and asked for his infant play.
The joy of his infancy is called beyond compare: even Brahma, Shiva and the sages long for it. Devotees love the Lord's play more than the Lord's majesty.
The smile is compassion: by his Vidya-maya he replaced dry knowledge with the sweetness of parental love (vatsalya).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Adhyatma Ramayana 1.3.29
commentaries.gist: There Kausalya likewise asks the Lord of the universe to withdraw his unearthly form and show his tender childhood.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the preciousness of ordinary moments with a baby: no greatness compares with being simply loved, and the sacred is met in the small.
misreadings: Not a rejection of God's greatness, only a preference for intimacy.
cautions: Centres a mother and newborn. Could be painful for a reader facing infertility or infant loss.
speaks_to: new parents
wanting closeness rather than achievement
devotion that prefers intimacy to awe
not_for: someone grieving a miscarriage, stillbirth or infant death
a reader struggling with infertility

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 198 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints '198'). NOT 1.186.
attribution_note: Narration (Shiva to Parvati within Yajnavalkya's frame). 'Tulsidas -> the reader' is a fair simplification.
translation_note: Good. 'बिगत बिनोद' means beyond play or amusement. Manas Piyush glosses it as 'free of play', which makes his infant play all the more striking.
context: After the naming ceremony the mothers cuddle the boys, sometimes in their laps and sometimes in a fine cradle, calling them pet names. Tulsidas pauses to marvel at who is lying there. The next lines describe the child's beauty limb by limb, then say Ram, father and mother of the world, gave joy to the people of Kosala.

key_terms.sense: stainless, beyond the qualities of matter

core_teaching: The infinite, unborn, all-pervading Absolute lies in a mother's lap, because love has won it over.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Love made the Lord give up his limits: the all-pervading came to one place, the vast became a child, the stainless played on earth, the unborn was born. All this is 'prem-bhakti-bas'.
Tulsidas's habit: whenever he describes the Lord's sweetness he adds a touch of majesty, so readers do not mistake him for an ordinary child.
One of three matching dohas in the childhood section (198, 201, 205). Each states the Lord's transcendence, then the love that binds him: first Kausalya's, then both parents', then the townspeople's.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: They see hidden childhood rites in these lines: Baijnath the infant's first showing to the sun, P. P. Pr. the first feeding of cow's milk.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that love brings the vast near: in caring for a child, a parent, or anyone, we hold something infinite.
misreadings: Not a reduction of God to a human infant: the verse insists on both.
cautions: Mother-and-infant imagery may be painful for readers facing infertility or infant loss.
speaks_to: new parents
the wonder of caring for a baby
feeling God is too vast to reach
not_for: someone grieving a baby or unable to have children

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 208, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 208, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.196.
translation_note: Good. 'गोसाईं' is 'my lord', addressing the sage. Note the 'late in life' in our setting is from the wider story, not this verse.
context: Vishwamitra comes to Ayodhya to ask for Ram (and Lakshman) to protect his sacrifice from demons. Dasharath offers land, cows, wealth, even his own body and life, but says he cannot give Ram. The sage is unmoved. Vasishtha explains things to the king, his doubts clear, and he hands both boys over with blessings.

key_terms.term: सब सुत प्रिय मोहि प्रान की नाईं
key_terms.sense: all my sons are dear to me as life
I cannot bring myself to give Ram

core_teaching: A parent's love makes some partings almost impossible, especially when the child faces danger. Yet growing up means the child must sometimes go.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He first calls all sons dear as life, so the sage cannot simply ask for another, then singles out Ram as dearer than life. Separation from Ram is worse than death to him, as the Ayodhya Kand will show.
He offered his body and life and the sage stayed silent. Realising breath cannot really be given, he tries again: the others he might give, but Ram is his very senses' master.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramcharan Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Panjabi: the eldest is most dear, and his life depends on seeing Ram. Mishra: the sons are like the breath, but Ram is the consciousness that gives breath life.
In Valmiki Dasharath admits he could not himself fight Ravana's forces, so how could he send boys? Tulsidas renders this as 'nothing is dearer than body and life'.

practical_reading: Readers apply it to parents letting children leave for school, hostel, a job or the army: the fear is real and honoured, and letting go becomes possible with wise counsel.
misreadings: Love that never lets go can hold a child back; in the story he does let Ram go.
speaks_to: parents sending a child away
fear for a child's safety
empty-nest feelings
not_for: a parent whose child has died, who may find the 'letting go' frame painful

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 261, chaupais 1-2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 261, half-lines 1-4'). NOT 1.247, and our text covers two chaupais, not one.
attribution_note: Narration, with the middle lines as Ram's reflection. Correct.
translation_note: Good. 'बैदेही' then 'जानकी': Manas Piyush notes the shift of name marks her near-faint, almost out of the body.
context: At the bride-choice, every king has failed to move Shiva's bow, and Janaka has despaired aloud. Ram rises at his guru's word and comes to the bow. He looks at the frozen crowd and then at Sita, who is in agony, each instant like an age. He reflects that help after the moment is useless, bows to his guru in his mind, lifts the bow in an instant and breaks it.

key_terms.sense: each instant passes like an aeon
what use is a lake of nectar after one has died?
what use is rain when the crops have dried?
once the moment is missed, what use is regret?

core_teaching: Help, love or action that comes after the moment is no help at all. Seeing someone suffering, act while it still matters.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Even a little relief on time (one inch of the bow moved) would have been water to the thirsty. Lifting and breaking it would be nectar, worthless if Sita has already died of grief. It cites a Dohavali couplet.
Ram looked on her as 'abode of grace', because she had staked love, not merit. The Lord is moved more by pure love than by austerities.
Commentators debate 'sudha': nectar revives the dead, so is it really useless? Some take 'sudha' as plain water, others (Unmani tika) as 'up to' or the Ganga. The point stands: timeliness.

practical_reading: Widely quoted as a maxim on timely action: a call, an apology, care for an ageing parent, treatment, a decision. Do it while it can still help.
misreadings: Not a reason for panic or recklessness: Ram acts calmly, after bowing to his guru.
Not a judgement on those who missed a moment through no fault of their own.
cautions: The images of dying of thirst and 'regret is useless' can wound someone who arrived too late for a loved one's death. Avoid for fresh grief or guilt.
speaks_to: procrastination
someone waiting for you to act
urgent decisions
caregiving
not_for: someone grieving a death they could not prevent or reach in time
a reader with anxiety who may hear only 'too late'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 274 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '274'). NOT 1.258.
translation_note: Good. Manuscripts differ: the oldest (1661) reads 'कथहिं प्रतापु' (talk of their prowess), others 'करहिं प्रलाप' (babble). The meaning is the same.
context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Parashurama has been reciting his feats: twenty-one times he rid the earth of kings, his axe killed Sahasrabahu. Lakshman tells him to go on if he is not satisfied, since a hero who reviles does not look well. Then he says this.

key_terms.sense: show it in deeds on the battlefield

core_teaching: The truly capable prove themselves in action, not words. Boasting in front of an opponent is the mark of insecurity.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's earlier jibes imply Parashurama is shameless, angry, a babbler. His pride in killing Sahasrabahu and ridding the earth of kshatriyas fuels his rage at a boy who does not fear him.
Notes the humour: Lakshman needles Parashurama's self-praise, then his abuse.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing a Subhashita
commentaries.gist: A verse on self-praise: virtues one claims for oneself bring no grace. Virtues others recognise do, so the wise never proclaim their own.

practical_reading: Teachers use the maxim at work and in sport: let results speak, and be wary of those who keep announcing what they can do.
misreadings: Not a ban on ever speaking about one's abilities (interviews, applications).
In context it is a taunt that inflames the sage, so the scene is not a model of how to say it.
cautions: Calls the boaster a coward, which is harsh if aimed at a reader. Use as a self-check, not a label.
speaks_to: impostor feelings next to loud colleagues
pressure to self-promote
competition and sport
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to speak up for themselves

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 276 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '276'). NOT 1.260.
translation_note: Good.
context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Lakshman has just told Parashurama that he spares him only because he is a Brahmin, and that he has grown big at home without facing a real warrior. The assembly cries out 'wrong!', Ram silences Lakshman with a glance, and seeing the sage's anger blazing up, speaks soothing words.

key_terms.sense: like oblations poured into a sacred fire

core_teaching: Sharp replies feed an angry person's fire like ghee. Cooling, humble words are what put it out.

commentaries.gist: All of Lakshman's replies are bitter, the last especially. Parashurama raises his axe and the hall cries out. Ram stops Lakshman by a sign, then speaks water-like words.
Lakshman, Vishvamitra and Ram had all asked forgiveness, yet Parashurama kept accusing. His capacity to forgive had gone: anger had destroyed forbearance.
Lakshman addresses him by his ancestor Bhrigu's name. Bhrigu kicked Vishnu, and his descendant raises an axe, so the name fits.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for conflict at home and work: when someone is angry, do not add fuel. Speak in a way that lowers the heat.
misreadings: Not a demand that people being abused must always placate their abuser.
Not a dismissal of Lakshman's loyalty: the issue is the effect of his words.
speaks_to: arguments with family or partners
managing an angry boss or customer
a sibling or friend who escalates conflicts
not_for: someone facing an abusive or violent person, where safety, not soothing words, is the priority
research_note: Our id and label use 1.260; the Gita Press number is 1.276. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 3 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 277 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '277'). NOT 1.261.
translation_note: Good.
context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Parashurama has just told Ram that his brother is a great sinner, and that Ram is not like him. Lakshman laughs and replies with this. He goes on with mock humility about the broken bow (next verse).

key_terms.sense: anger is the root of wrongdoing

core_teaching: Anger is the root of wrongdoing: in its grip people do what they should not and turn against everyone.

commentaries.who: Ramcharan Mishra, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's laughter signals irony: a calm reply that is really a counter-thrust.

It answers 'your brother is a great sinner': if anger is sin's root and anger rides on you, who is the sinner? It links Hanuman's reflection on anger in Valmiki 5.55.5-6: the angry may kill even their guru.
Implies that anger is why Parashurama cannot recognise Ram, and why he speaks harshly to the one his own guru worships.

practical_reading: Teachers quote the maxim on its own: notice anger rising, because most regrettable words and acts begin there.
misreadings: Not a teaching that all anger is sinful, including anger at injustice.
In the scene Lakshman uses it as a taunt, which inflames rather than cools. Do not present it as a model of how to calm someone.
speaks_to: a quick temper
regret after an outburst
parents and teachers modelling calm
not_for: someone whose justified anger at abuse or injustice is being dismissed

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 278, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 278, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.262.
translation_note: Good. The tone is mock courtesy: next he offers to call a good craftsman to glue the bow back if Parashurama loves it so much.
context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Right after saying anger is the root of sin, Lakshman puts on a show of humility: I am your servant, be kind, a broken bow won't mend through anger, your feet must ache, sit down. The jibes continue until Ram steps in again.

key_terms.sense: a broken bow won't join because you're angry

core_teaching: As a saying: anger cannot undo what is done. In the scene it is mockery that inflames rather than calms.

commentaries.gist: Paraphrases the lines and the one after: if the bow is so dear, let us call a skilled craftsman to join it, which is plainly sarcastic.
The whole exchange is a play of retort and counter-retort. Lakshman's laughter marks irony beneath polite words.

practical_reading: The half-line 'a broken thing won't mend through anger' is used on its own as gentle advice to stop raging over what cannot be undone, but say it kindly, not as Lakshman does.
misreadings: Not a model of how to talk to an angry person: in context it is sarcasm that stokes the fire.
Not 'just get over it' for a real loss.
cautions: Sarcastic tone. If quoted to someone grieving a loss ('it won't mend'), it can sound dismissive.
speaks_to: rumination over a past mistake or loss
family arguments about something broken or lost
not_for: someone grieving a death or a broken relationship
an angry reader who would hear mockery
