verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 338, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 338, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.318.
translation_note: Good. 'महामरजाद ग्यान की' means the great boundary or dignity of wisdom, like a river's banks overflowing.
context: After the four weddings, the brides are leaving Mithila for Ayodhya. The queens weep, and even the parrots and mynas Sita raised cry out her name. Then Janaka and his brother come. Janaka, renowned as the most detached of sages, sees Sita and breaks down. Later Janaka collects himself and sees them off.

key_terms.sense: the great banks of his wisdom gave way

core_teaching: Even the most detached and wise heart breaks open at a beloved daughter's leaving. Love sweeps past the boundaries of wisdom, and Tulsidas honours it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: His tears come from love of Janaki, not delusion (compare Ayodhya 286). Others' composure merely slipped. Janaka's fled, because his love was greater.
'Was called supremely detached' suggests that today it did not show. First his composure went, and with it knowledge and dispassion.
That love overflows the banks of knowledge shows the beauty of knowledge: it is love's worth that even the wisest bow to it.
Renunciation is practised to reach the Lord. How could it hold at the parting from Sita, who is herself that goal?

practical_reading: Used at weddings and send-offs: grief at a child's leaving is not weakness or a failure of wisdom. Even the wise cry.
misreadings: Not a criticism of Janaka or of detachment.
speaks_to: a daughter's or son's wedding and leaving home
parents sending children abroad
people embarrassed by their own tears
not_for: a parent estranged from a child, for whom the warm embrace may sting
research_note: Our id and label use 1.318; the Gita Press number is 1.338.3. Confirmed in Manas Piyush (Gita Press) vol. 3 and in a Gita Press-numbered text dataset.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 10, chaupai 3-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 10, half-lines 5-8'). NOT 2.11.
attribution_note: Lines 1-3 are Ram's inner thought (the poet frames it as wonder/unease arising in Ram's heart after Vasishtha leaves); the last line is Tulsidas's own prayer, not Ram's. Our translation already marks this.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Eldest alone is crowned' fits; Manas Piyush stresses 'बिसमउ' carries wonder mixed with doubt and worry. Growse renders the last line's कुटिलाई as 'unworthy suspicion', most commentators as crookedness/selfishness.
context: Dasharath has decided to make Ram crown prince, and Vasishtha has just come to tell Ram to keep vows for the next day's ceremony. As soon as the guru leaves, Ram's first feeling is not pride but disquiet: everything in the brothers' lives has been shared, so crowning only the eldest seems the one blot on a spotless line. Lakshman arrives right after, and Ram welcomes him with loving words.

key_terms.sense: wonder mixed with unease and doubt
the eldest anointed, brothers left aside
crookedness, selfish twist of the heart

core_teaching: True affection is uneasy when it is favoured over those it grew up with. Tulsidas holds up Ram's loving regret as a medicine for the selfishness in a devotee's own heart.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The two lines are ordered deliberately: birth, meals, sleep and play are shared bodily life; ear-piercing, sacred thread and marriage are shared rites. Ram is troubled that Bharat and Shatrughna are absent and not even informed.
Primogeniture is family custom, but Ram means the brothers should share in rule too, each with a role; he will not accept the throne in his brothers' absence.

commentaries.who: Vedantabhushan Pt. Ramkumardas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Raises the objection: Manu's law favours the eldest, other lawgivers favour equal shares. Ram calls the custom unfair yet still honours the received order, so his dignity stays intact.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi and Ramchandra Shukla, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Not grieving for others when you yourself rise is itself 'crookedness' for a devotee; contemplating Ram's simple fairness slowly makes a crooked person straight.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for sibling fairness: when you are singled out (a promotion, an inheritance, a parent's favour), let the first feeling be concern for those who shared the road with you. The Vinayaki tika cited in Manas Piyush applies it directly to brothers who grab the larger share of property.
misreadings: Not a rejection of responsibility or of the eldest's role: Ram does accept his father's plan.
Not a call to refuse every honour; it is about the spirit in which you receive it.
cautions: Can sting for a reader who is the overlooked sibling in a real inheritance or family dispute; frame it as a picture of how a fair heart feels, not as proof that their sibling is wrong.
speaks_to: someone promoted or rewarded above siblings, friends or co-founders
parents dividing property or attention among children
siblings who grew up close and now face unequal fortunes
not_for: a reader in active conflict with a sibling who took everything, on the day of the hurt
only children or people estranged from their siblings, without reframing
research_note: Our id/label (2.11, chaupai 3) does not match Gita Press numbering (10.5-8). Our setting also says Ram was 'told he alone will be crowned'; more precisely Vasishtha told him to prepare for coronation as crown prince the next day.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 22, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 22 (1-3)' and '(4-7)'). NOT 2.23.
attribution_note: First half is the narrator's comment on Manthara's speech; the second half begins Manthara's words to Kaikeyi. 'Narrator' is right for the image.
translation_note: Faithful. Manas Piyush glosses माहुर as poison and घोरी as 'dissolved/mixed in'.
context: Kaikeyi has just sworn she would throw herself in a well at Manthara's word, even give up son and husband. The poet pictures Manthara as a butcher sharpening the knife of deceit on the stone of her heart, while Kaikeyi, like a sacrificial animal, grazes on green grass without seeing her doom. Then comes this line, and Manthara at once reminds Kaikeyi of the two boons Dasharath owes her.

key_terms.sense: soft to hear, harsh in outcome

core_teaching: Words that are sweet to hear can carry a deadly result. Commentators read the image as a warning about flattering counsel that feeds our fears and grudges.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: As sherbet is poured into the mouth of the animal to be sacrificed, Manthara pours honeyed poison into Kaikeyi; the speech is soft first, ruinous after.
Valmiki calls Manthara 'pāpadarśinī', sharp-eyed for evil; Tulsidas turns that into the images of the knife, the grazing victim and honey laced with poison.
The 'sacrifice' is Kaikeyi's own good name: winning the boons brings her lasting disgrace, which Tulsidas elsewhere calls worse than death.

practical_reading: Used as a test for advice: does it soothe me now and leave me worse later? Teachers apply it to gossip, manipulative friends and counsel that inflames rivalry inside families.
misreadings: Not a claim that all gentle speech is suspect.
Not a verdict that women or servants are schemers; it is about one manipulative speech.
cautions: A reader who was manipulated may hear blame for 'falling for it'; the poet's sympathy here is partly with Kaikeyi as the victim.
speaks_to: someone realising a 'well-wisher' has been feeding their worst fears
family rivalries stoked by a third party
checking advice before a big decision
not_for: a reader grieving a betrayal by someone close, as a first reading: it can deepen suspicion of everyone
research_note: Our prasang summary is accurate.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 42, chaupai 1 (lines 1-2) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 42 (1-2)'). Number matches.
translation_note: Faithful. Dataset reads 'बिधि सब बिधि मोहि सनमुख आजू'; 'fate favouring me in every way' is right (बिधि = Brahma/Providence).
context: Ram has entered Dasharath's chamber to find him collapsed, and Kaikeyi has laid out the two boons. In the preceding doha Ram lists the gains: time with sages in the forest, his father's command, and her own consent. Here he adds the fourth, Bharat ruling, and says only a fool would miss such a chance. He then confesses his one real pain: seeing his father so distraught.

key_terms.sense: Providence faces me favourably in every way

core_teaching: Ram reframes a loss of the throne as a cluster of gains: holy company, obedience to his father, his stepmother's wish fulfilled and his brother's good. Commentators insist this is his sincere view, not a polite mask.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (citing Vandan Pathak), in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The four reasons map onto the four aims of life: sages' company brings moksha, the father's word dharma, Kaikeyi's consent kama, and Bharat's rule artha.

'Dear as life' means: people strive for the comfort of their life-breath, and here, without effort, the one dear as life receives the kingdom. Cites Valmiki 2.26 on Bharat and Shatrughna being dearer than life.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram repeats the same reasons later to Valmiki, which shows they were not said merely to please Kaikeyi.
People want a kingdom for the sake of loved ones' happiness; if Bharat gets it, Ram loses nothing. Missing such a moment would be the truest foolishness.

practical_reading: A model for meeting a lost role or promotion by naming honestly what the new path offers and rejoicing in a loved one's gain. Teachers stress it is a choice of perspective made while still feeling the pain (Ram's next lines show his distress at his father).
misreadings: Grace in loss is not pretending it doesn't hurt (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand that a reader be glad about an unjust loss imposed on them.
cautions: Could feel like toxic positivity to someone freshly laid off or displaced; pair with Ram's admission of grief in the next lines.
speaks_to: someone who lost a promotion, role or inheritance to a sibling or colleague they love
people trying to see a forced change as an opening
not_for: victims of real injustice who need validation first
a reader in acute grief

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 42 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4; Growse 'Doha 42'). Number matches.
translation_note: Our Awadhi text has 'सहज सकल'; Gita Press, Manas Piyush and the dataset read 'सहज सरल' (naturally straightforward). Fix the text; the translation 'simple by nature' already follows सरल. Manas Piyush notes Nagari Pracharini reads 'जोंक जिमि'.
context: Ram has just told Kaikeyi, with full sincerity, why exile is a gain for him and asked only why his father is so distressed. Kaikeyi, already set on her course, hears every gentle word as a ploy to soften her. The poet answers with the leech image: the water is level, the crookedness is in the leech.
core_teaching: How we hear words depends on the mind that hears them. When the mind is twisted, even straight speech looks crooked; the fault lies in the hearer, not the speech.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The water has no fault; the leech moves crookedly. Likewise the fault is not in Ram's words but in Kaikeyi's 'kumati'. Raghus do not dress up speech, so Ram's words could not be crafted.
Kaikeyi assumed Ram was charming her with soft words so she would withdraw the exile, and resolved not to be fooled.
Ram's speech is full of reasoning, which is why a suspicious hearer could take it as cleverness.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the doha as the wicked queen giving his straightforward words 'a perverse twist', like a leech that moves crookedly however smooth the water.

practical_reading: Applied to conflict and suspicion: when someone keeps reading your plain words as manipulation, the problem may be in the lens, not the message; and when you find yourself doing it, check your own lens.
misreadings: Not licence to dismiss every criticism of your words as the other person's 'twisted mind'.
cautions: Can be weaponised in a relationship ('you just hear everything wrong'); frame it as self-examination first.
speaks_to: someone whose good intentions keep being misread
a reader noticing their own suspicion colouring everything
family conflict where trust has broken down
not_for: someone being gaslit, who may be told their accurate perception is the 'crooked' one

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 51 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 '॥५१॥'). Growse numbers it Doha 50, which matches our id. NOT Gita Press 2.50.
translation_note: Faithful. अलान is the post or shackle used to tether a newly caught elephant (Manas Piyush cites Amarakosha: 'alānaṁ gaja-bandhanam'). 'Newly captured' matters: an old captive elephant no longer longs for the forest.
context: Ayodhya's people are lamenting and cursing Kaikeyi, but Ram walks to his mother Kausalya with a cheerful face and 'fourfold eagerness', his one fear (that the king might hold him back) gone. The doha explains his lightness: kingship had been a tether. Right after, Kausalya, still thinking it is coronation day, blesses him and asks when the auspicious hour is.
core_teaching: Ram never wanted the throne for himself; losing it felt like freedom. Commentators read it as a sign of his inner detachment and of the forest being where his real work lies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: An elephant long in captivity stops wanting the forest; a newly caught one suffers in bondage and longs to roam free. Ram's mind is the new one.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The coronation was arranged against Ram's own wish; its cancellation increased the joy of one who is by nature a treasury of bliss.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha 12.7
commentaries.gist: Kalidasa too says Ram wept when given the earth and gladly took the command to go to the forest.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a young elephant with kingship for its chain, the news of exile being the chain's breaking.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the relief that can come with losing a role we never wanted: a job, a title, an expectation. It invites the reader to ask which of their 'honours' are really tethers.
misreadings: Losing a role can free you; that does not make every loss a gift (our misuse note is right).
Not a case for dodging duty: Ram embraces a harder duty.
cautions: Ill-suited to someone devastated by a job loss or forced eviction they did not want.
speaks_to: someone relieved after leaving a role that never fit
a person freed from family expectations of a career or position
people choosing a simpler life
not_for: a reader who has just lost something they deeply wanted
job loss with financial distress
research_note: Numbering: our id follows Growse/one older numbering; Gita Press has 51.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 55, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 55, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 2.54.
attribution_note: First line is the narrator; the second line is Kausalya's inner reasoning. Fine as 'Narrator'.
translation_note: Faithful. छुछुंदरि is the musk shrew (often called muskrat). The folk belief behind the image, per Manas Piyush: a snake that seizes one dies if it swallows it and goes blind if it lets go.
context: Ram has told Kausalya, who was preparing for his coronation, that he must go to the forest. She cannot hold him back nor tell him to go. If she keeps him, dharma is broken and it looks like a quarrel with Bharat; if she sends him, the loss is huge. Then, remembering a wife's duty and that Ram and Bharat are both her sons, she steadies herself and tells him he has done well, for a father's command crowns all duties.

key_terms.sense: the snake that has seized a musk shrew

core_teaching: Duty and love can trap a good heart in a position where every option costs something. The verse names that bind honestly before Kausalya chooses.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya is the snake, Ram the shrew: keeping him home is swallowing (loss of dharma, disgrace), sending him is releasing (fourteen years of weeping, the 'blindness').
In the end the snake swallows and dies; so Kausalya chose death over abandoning dharma, since her husband, her life, would die.
The snake drops the shrew in water to escape; so Kausalya left the matter to Kaikeyi's decree, keeping both her love and her duty.
'Brothers' conflict' does not mean Ram and Bharat would fight; Kausalya fears Kaikeyi would read any restraint as setting Ram against Bharat.

practical_reading: Used for any parent or caregiver caught between two goods: a child's calling versus wanting them close, a dying parent versus a job. Naming the bind honestly is the first step before choosing.
misreadings: Not saying every dilemma has a clean right answer.
Not a teaching that a mother's love is a weakness to be overcome.
cautions: The snake-and-shrew image is earthy and folk-zoological; explain it gently. The next lines resolve in favour of duty, which can sound like 'love must lose'.
speaks_to: parents letting a child move far away for study, work or marriage
caregivers torn between family and career
anyone stuck where both choices hurt
not_for: someone who wants to be told what to do; the verse only describes the bind
research_note: Growse (6th ed.) also renders it as 'a snake with a musk rat'.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 56 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 '॥५६॥'). Growse numbers it Doha 55, matching our id. NOT Gita Press 2.55.
translation_note: Acceptable, but the phrase झूठ सनेहु is read two ways. Our version (I won't press you out of a false, self-serving affection) follows the common reading. Several commentators in Manas Piyush read it as self-reproach: 'my love must be false, since I still live after hearing you go.' Growse: she will not press 'with a show of love beyond what I really feel'. Keep our wording; the writer should know the self-reproach shade.
context: Kausalya has steadied herself: a father's command crowns all duties, and if it were only Dasharath's she might forbid it, but Kaikeyi's wish counts too, so the forest will be like a hundred Ayodhyas, with forest gods for parents. She admits she cannot ask to come along without unsettling him. This doha is her decision: no insisting, only a plea to keep the bond. Then she blesses him (the next chaupai) and collapses at his feet.

key_terms.sense: inflating a false or showy affection
honouring the tie of a mother
do not let the memory (of me) slip

core_teaching: Real love sometimes means not using love as leverage. Kausalya lets her son go with her blessing and asks only to stay in his heart.

commentaries.who: Munshi Roshanlal, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya calls her own love false because her life did not leave her on hearing of the exile; even so, she asks Ram to honour the mother-tie from his side and remember her.
Tulsidas condenses Valmiki's line where Kausalya asks Ram not to give up being her son, and makes it more piercing.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: At the level of ultimate truth her attachment is illusory, yet in everyday reality she is mother and he is son, and that should not be forgotten.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: she will not press her suit with a show of love beyond what she feels, and prays he will not forget her.

practical_reading: Read at send-offs: a parent can bless a child's leaving instead of guilt-tripping them into staying, and still say plainly 'don't forget me'. Love that releases is not love that has stopped.
misreadings: Not a claim that a parent's grief at parting is 'fake'.
Not advice to suppress feelings: she voices her grief in the next lines.
cautions: For a parent whose child has cut contact, 'don't forget me' may hurt; for a parent who has lost a child to death, the parting imagery can be raw.
speaks_to: parents of children leaving for study, work, marriage or abroad
adult children who feel guilt about leaving ageing parents
anyone tempted to hold someone back with emotional pressure
not_for: bereaved parents
parents estranged from a child, without care
research_note: Numbering follows Growse; Gita Press 2.56.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 57, chaupai 1 (lines 1-2) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 57 (1-3)'). NOT 2.56.
translation_note: Mostly faithful. गोसाईं is read two ways: most commentators take it as Kausalya addressing Ram ('my lord'); Vijayanand Tripathi, whom Manas Piyush prefers, takes it as Narayan, a third protector alongside gods and ancestors. Our line leaves out the next line, which makes the point explicit: so act that you come back while everyone is still alive.
context: Right after deciding not to hold Ram back, Kausalya blesses him. The image of eyelids is followed by another: the fourteen-year term is water and his loved ones are fish who will survive only while it lasts. She asks him, being compassionate and steadfast in dharma, to find a way to return while all are alive, then breaks down and clings to his feet. Ram lifts her and consoles her; Sita then arrives.

key_terms.sense: as the eyelids guard the eye
a mine of compassion, bearer of dharma's yoke

core_teaching: A mother's blessing for safe keeping, joined to a plea: the family's life is tied to his return on time. Love blesses the journey and still asks the traveller to come home.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The eye is the tenderest organ; the lids shut instantly at the slightest speck and close it in sleep, trusting no one. So should the gods guard Ram.
The ancestors are the lower lid and the gods the upper; together they protect the pupil.
'Gosain' here is not an address to Ram but means Narayan, who along with gods and ancestors is asked to protect him. Manas Piyush finds this the better reading.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Fish die when water runs out: the family will survive only until the term ends. Ram, knowing his father will not live, gives no answer to the plea to return while all live.

practical_reading: A model blessing for anyone setting out on a long absence: wish them protected, and tell them honestly how much their return matters.
misreadings: Not a pressure tactic; it is a blessing that names the family's dependence.
cautions: The 'fish without water' image implies the family may die before the return; Dasharath does. Gentle handling for readers with ailing parents far away.
speaks_to: a parent blessing a child going abroad, to the army, or to a long posting
families separated by migration
a traveller who needs to feel held
not_for: someone whose parent died while they were away
readers wrestling with guilt about not returning in time
research_note: Our prasang is null; it belongs with rcm.p.ram_kausalya. Manas Piyush cites Valmiki 2.25 for Kausalya's longer blessing listing gods.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 68, chaupai 4 (lines 7-8) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 68, half-lines 7-8'). Growse prints the following doha as 'Doha 67', matching our id. NOT Gita Press 2.67.
translation_note: Faithful. Manas Piyush identifies the 'lovely pair' as Ram and Sita.
context: Sita has just won Ram's consent to come to the forest. Ram comforts her and bows to his mother, who asks him to return soon and end the people's grief and not forget his 'hard-hearted' mother. These lines are her last questions to fate before the doha where she longs to call him 'calf' and 'darling' and hold him again. Ram consoles her in many ways; then Sita bows to her.

key_terms.sense: the good day, the blessed hour

core_teaching: A mother's honest fear at parting: she hopes for the day of reunion but doubts she will live to see it. Tulsidas lets grief speak without correcting it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: While Ram was home her 'dasha' was good; his leaving marks a bad turn. 'Will it turn again' means: will good days return so these eyes see the pair again?
'When will that hour come' implies fourteen years is very long; despairing of living that long, she asks whether the mother will still be alive to see his face.
Compares Tulsidas's Gitavali songs where Kausalya asks how she will bear the house without her child and his voice.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the lines as Kausalya hoping God may change her lot and asking when the happy day will come that she lives to see his moon-like face.

practical_reading: Gives words to parents and grandparents who fear they won't live to see a far-away child return. It validates the fear rather than dismissing it.
misreadings: Not a prediction of death; it is a mother's fear voiced.
cautions: Directly raises the fear of dying before a reunion; avoid for a reader whose parent died during a separation, unless they seek it.
speaks_to: elderly parents of children abroad
families facing long separations (deployment, migration, prison terms)
adult children who hear this fear from their parents
not_for: readers bereaved of a parent they could not see before death
someone needing hope rather than lament
research_note: Our setting says Ram, Sita and Lakshman take leave; Lakshman is not present in this scene (he goes to Sumitra at 2.73-75). The setting should say Ram and Sita.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 74, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 74, half-lines 3-4'). Growse prints the doha as 'Doha 73', matching our id. NOT Gita Press 2.73.
translation_note: Faithful.
context: Lakshman has come to his mother afraid she will stop him going. Sumitra, first shaken, then steadies herself and tells him: your mother is now Sita and your father Ram. Home is wherever Ram lives, as day is wherever the sun shines. She goes on: elders and gods are to be served like one's own life, but Ram is the life of life; go with him and reap the gain of being born.

key_terms.sense: day is wherever the sun shines

core_teaching: Home is not a place but the presence of the one you love and serve. Commentators read it devotionally: where Ram is, there is everything that home gives.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note (Gita Press), citing Valmiki 2.37.29 and 2.40.9
commentaries.gist: Vasishtha says the realm will be wherever Ram lives, and Valmiki's Sumitra tells Lakshman to think of the forest as Ayodhya. Tulsidas's line condenses both.
Ayodhya without Ram is like night; the poet later says Ayodhya looked like a dark night of doom. And Lakshman truly never thought of home again.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sumitra's words carry spiritual meaning: worldly parents love with some self-interest; Sita (Vaidehi, free of body-attachment) and Ram love without it.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: where Rama dwells there is Avadh, and wherever the sun's light is, there is day.

practical_reading: Used for migrants, newly-weds and families who move: home is made by people and love, not by an address. Also used devotionally: where God is remembered, there is home.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of one's parents or birthplace; Sumitra herself honours elders in the next line.
Not an instruction to follow anyone anywhere regardless of harm.
cautions: For someone who has no 'people' nearby (isolated migrants, the bereaved), 'home is where your people are' can sharpen loneliness; the devotional reading may land better.
speaks_to: people moving cities or countries
newly married people leaving their parents' home
families relocating for a loved one's work or care
not_for: someone who has lost the person who was their 'home'
people in controlling relationships being pressured to follow

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 75, chaupai 3 (lines 5-6) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 75, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 2.74.
translation_note: Faithful. Manas Piyush glosses राग as worldly attachment, रोष as anger, इरिषा as envy, मद as pride, मोह as delusion.
context: Sumitra has told Lakshman that a mother is truly blessed only if her son loves Ram, and that the highest fruit of all good deeds is natural love for Sita and Ram's feet. Here she names the five enemies of that service, then says he will lack nothing in the forest with Ram and Sita as parents, and gives her one instruction: do whatever keeps Ram from hardship. Lakshman leaves at once, like a deer escaping a snare.
core_teaching: Service done well needs a clean heart: Sumitra names five inner disturbances that spoil it and asks for service in thought, word and act.

commentaries.gist: Each is applied to Lakshman's service: no attachment to home and kin, no anger even at hard words (he stays calm when Sita rebukes him), no envy ('we are both princes'), no pride, no forgetting who Ram is.
After the five she says 'every kind of distortion', since there are many more; mind, deed and word must all stay pure in service.
Service of mind is keeping the moment of service in view; of word, asking fitting orders and speaking sweetly; of deed, the actual work.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the list as lust, passion, envy, pride and delusion, followed by serving them in heart, word and deed.

practical_reading: A parent's parting advice that works for any young adult leaving home or starting a demanding role: guard against attachment, anger, envy, pride and confusion, and serve wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not a claim that all feeling is bad; the target is being 'ruled' by these states.
Service here is devotional; it is not a mandate for self-erasure toward any boss or partner.
cautions: 'Not even in a dream' sets an impossible bar if read literally; frame it as an aim.
speaks_to: young adults leaving home
caregivers and people in service roles
anyone starting work alongside a sibling or mentor where envy could creep in
not_for: someone in an exploitative relationship being told to serve without complaint
research_note: Our id follows Growse's grouping; Gita Press 2.75.3.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 92, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 92 (1-3)' and '(4-8)', the start of the 'Lakshman Gita'). Growse prints the closing doha as 'Doha 90', matching our id. NOT Gita Press 2.90.
attribution_note: First line is the narrator introducing Lakshman; the teaching line is Lakshman to Nishadraj Guha. Correct.
translation_note: Faithful. Growse: no man is the cause of another's joy or sorrow; all is the fruit of one's own actions.
context: On the first night of exile at Shringverpur, Guha sees Ram and Sita asleep on a bed of grass and, grieving, calls Kaikeyi a dull-witted woman who has become an axe to the solar dynasty. Lakshman, keeping watch, answers softly so as not to wake Ram. He goes on: union and separation, friend and foe, wealth and loss are snares of delusion, like a dream where a beggar becomes king; so do not be angry or blame anyone; true waking is detachment and love for Ram.

key_terms.sense: experiencing the fruit of one's own deeds
steeped in knowledge, dispassion and devotion

core_teaching: No other person is the true source of our joy or sorrow; we live out the results of our own actions. The point, in context, is to stop Guha's anger and blame, then lead him toward detachment and devotion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guha blamed Kaikeyi for giving sorrow; Lakshman answers from the Mimamsa view that action is primary. He speaks sweetly so as not to hurt Guha or wake Ram, and calls a lowly boatman 'brother'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Adhyatma Ramayana 2.6.4-8
commentaries.gist: The parallel verse calls it bad thinking to believe another gives us joy or sorrow; one should accept what comes from one's own past acts and keep the mind steady.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Absorbing this principle cures hatred, envy, fault-finding and blaming others, and increases one's capacity to bear pain. Worldly gain and loss follow past karma; spiritual good comes by effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The rule is said for all beings, not for Ram, whose deeds are free play, not karmic fruit.

practical_reading: Applied to blame and resentment: instead of locating all your pain in one person, look at the whole chain of causes, including your own part, and stop feeding anger. It returns your peace to your own hands.
misreadings: Not 'you deserve your suffering' (our misuse note is right).
Not an excuse for wrongdoers: commentators say Kaikeyi will bear her own deeds' fruit.
Not a reason to stop seeking justice or protection from harm.
cautions: Karma language can feel like victim-blaming to someone abused, assaulted, bereaved by violence or chronically ill. Do not use for those readers.
Rebirth/past-life karma underlies the traditional reading; keep it light for general readers.
speaks_to: someone stuck in resentment at a relative or ex-partner
family members blaming one person for a shared misfortune
people who want to stop handing their peace to others
not_for: victims of abuse, violence or injustice
fresh grief, especially after an accident or someone else's negligence
people with depression prone to self-blame
research_note: This and 2.91.1 are the core of the 'Lakshman Gita' (Gita Press 92.3-93.8).

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 93, chaupai 1 (lines 1-2) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 93 (1-2)'). Growse places it after his 'Doha 90'. NOT Gita Press 2.91.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Thinking this through' refers to the preceding doha: a beggar who becomes king in a dream gains nothing on waking.
context: Lakshman has just told Guha that every pair of opposites (union and separation, friend and foe, heaven and hell) is rooted in delusion, and that the world is like a dream from which the waking gain or lose nothing. From this he draws the practical conclusion: no anger, no needless blame. He continues that only yogis detached from the senses are awake in this night, and that the highest good is love for Ram in thought, word and deed.

key_terms.sense: do not lay blame in vain

core_teaching: Seeing life's ups and downs as a dream seen in the night of delusion, one drops anger and needless blame. Waking up means detachment and love for God.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guha blamed Kaikeyi, so Lakshman says blame no one in vain. People fault whoever they are angry with; think the matter through and you will see no one is truly at fault. Thus far knowledge; dispassion follows.
In a dream there is no one else: you yourself become enemy, friend, loss and gain. On waking no one counts the dream-enemy as an enemy, so neither anger nor blame makes sense.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'I and mine, you and yours' is the main dream; still, as one thorn removes another, the guru-disciple relation is a useful dream to end a binding one.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: reasoning thus, be not angry with anyone nor vainly blame anyone; all are sleepers in a night of delusion seeing many dreams.

practical_reading: Used to cool anger: before blaming, ask whether you are reacting inside a 'dream' of me-and-mine. Many teachers apply it to family quarrels and long-held grudges.
misreadings: Not blaming is not the same as excusing harm (our misuse note is right).
'The world is a dream' is not a licence to ignore suffering or responsibility.
cautions: Calling a loss 'a dream' can feel dismissive to someone grieving or wronged; avoid for fresh loss.
Rests on Vedantic metaphysics; present as perspective, not as a claim that the reader's pain is unreal.
speaks_to: someone ready to let go of a grudge
family members caught in mutual blame
people whose anger is hurting themselves most
not_for: abuse survivors
fresh grief
someone whose anger is a needed signal of real injustice

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 95, chaupai 3 (lines 5-6) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 95 (3-6)'). Growse places it before his 'Doha 93', matching our id. NOT Gita Press 2.93.
translation_note: Faithful. आगम निगम पुरान = tantra/agama, Veda and Puranas. Growse: 'no virtue equal to truth'.
context: The morning after the night at Shringverpur, the minister Sumantra begs Ram, on the king's behalf, to return so Ayodhya is not left orphaned. Ram raises him and reminds him of Shibi, Dadhichi, Harishchandra, Rantideva and Bali, who bore countless hardships for dharma. Truth is the highest dharma, and he has got it cheaply; abandoning it would bring disgrace, which for an honoured person is worse than a million deaths.
core_teaching: Keeping one's word (here, a father's promise) is the highest dharma. Ram adds that it has come to him cheaply compared to the great kings who suffered for it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Sumantra might say those kings' trials were extreme, so why suffer? Ram answers that truth has no equal, with scripture as proof; making a father's word true crowns all duties.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Valmiki 2.14 and 2.109
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Kaikeyi and Ram (answering Jabali) say truth is the root of all dharma; gifts, sacrifice, austerity and the Vedas rest on it.
'Easily obtained': kings gave their lives for ordinary dharma, while Ram gets the highest by a few years in the forest; to drop it would make him look a coward in dharma.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: there is no virtue equal to truth, as Vedas, Shastras and Puranas declare; he has reached it by an easy road, and abandoning it would spread his disgrace through earth, heaven and hell.

practical_reading: Used for integrity under pressure: when loved ones urge you to break a commitment for comfort, remember that keeping your word is itself the treasure, and often costs less than you fear.
misreadings: Not an argument to keep a promise that harms others or was extracted by abuse.
Not a call to value reputation above people; the following line's stress on disgrace is cultural and should not dominate.

translation_note: Faithful. बनि is an Awadhi word for wages (Manas Piyush, after Deenji); दावा = forest fire, applied to faults, sorrows and poverty alike.
context: On the far bank of the Ganga, Ram feels awkward that he has nothing to give the boatman who bowed to him. Sita, reading his mind, gladly takes off her jewelled ring; Ram tells Kevat to take his fare, and Kevat clutches his feet. He says he has already received everything, wants nothing more, and will accept whatever Ram gives on the way back. Unable to make him take anything, Ram dismisses him with the boon of pure devotion.

key_terms.sense: the wildfire of faults, sorrows and poverty

core_teaching: Kevat's real wage is having served and touched the Lord; no fee could match it. Commentators read the refusal as the mark of desireless devotion that receives pure bhakti.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Clutching the feet means: after seeing you, why would I want worldly enjoyment? Don't cheat me with a ring. Faults are the cause, sorrows the effect; both burned away by touching the feet, and poverty, the worst sorrow, too.
He had laboured through many births, scorched by sorrow; today, working for Ram, his belly was filled. Plainly: a lifetime ferrying, but today's fare exceeds all.
Deferring payment: he had sworn to take no fare; or he keeps Ram in his debt so he returns to this ghat; or each ferried the other across, so they are even.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (on the doha)
commentaries.gist: Ram, Lakshman and Sita pressed gifts; because he took none, he received pure devotion. Only the desireless receive such grace.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: he has laboured a length of years, but today God has given him his wages in full.

practical_reading: Applied to work and gratitude: some moments of service pay more than money, and the joy of having helped can itself be full payment. It honours working people's dignity.
misreadings: Not an argument that workers should not be paid or should refuse wages.
Not a romanticisation of poverty.
cautions: For readers struggling financially, 'paid in full without money' could ring hollow; emphasise gratitude and dignity, not giving up earnings.
